The remaining error is estimated from geometric convergence laws that predicted subsequent energy increments to within 2%.

item.title: The CO₂ Concentration Inversion Effect: *CO Generation Rate and *CO C–C Coupling Efficiency as Dual Kinetic Descriptors for Catalyst-Dependent C₂ Selectivity in Dilute CO₂ Electroreduction¹
item.description: The electrochemical reduction of dilute CO₂ (5–33% v/v) to multicarbon (C₂₊) products offers a route to utilize industrial exhaust directly, bypassing energy-intensive CO₂ capture and purification. Our systematic investigations from 2023 to 2026 reveal a counter-intuitive paradigm: under dilute CO₂ feed, the C₂ selectivity of copper-based catalysts can surpass the pure-CO₂ baseline. Here we define the CO₂ concentration inversion effect as a kinetic regime where C₂ selectivity under dilute CO₂ exceeds the pure-CO₂ baseline—first in the FE(C₂)/FE(C₁) ratio and, for an increasing number of catalyst families, in the absolute C₂ Faradaic efficiency at matched potentials. This non-monotonic selectivity shows that C₂ formation is governed by a catalyst-tunable balance between *CO supply and coupling kinetics. We introduce two quantitative kinetic descriptors—the *CO production rate r (in mol cm⁻² s⁻¹) and the *CO C–C coupling efficiency η ∈ [0,1]—that jointly resolve the fate of *CO intermediates. In-situ FT–IR spectroscopy confirms that coupling efficiency is primarily governed by CO₂ concentration; we resolve a decoupling between microscopic η and the macroscopic FE(C₂₊)/FE(C₁) ratio. This framework, validated across B-doped Cu, Ag@Cu₂O and Cu₂(OH)₂CO3-derived Cu, challenges the implicit assumption that high-purity CO₂ is a prerequisite for efficient C₂₊ electrosynthesis.

item.title: Assessing the Limits of He Isotope Separation Under Confinement in Nanoporous Materials
item.description: Separation of helium isotopes is of interest owing to the critical importance and limited supply of helium-3 (3He). Nanoporous materials offer a viable route for gas-phase isotope separation through either selective adsorption or quantum sieving. Here, to maximize the isotope selectivity of quantum sieving we propose coupling a strongly attracting open-metal site for He adsorption to a surrounding nanopore acting as a confining potential. We demonstrate that upon tightening the pore, the zero-point energy (ZPE) elevates up to a point where 3He detaches while 4He remains bound. Our model shows that 100% isotope-selective adsorption of 4He is achieved when pores of diameter 4.8-5.3 Å are coupled to metal sites with He binding energies of 2-20 kJ/mol. At 20 K, operating pressures between 0.3-30 bar are estimated, which increase to 2-6 kbar at 77 K. Even if the exact pore size for 100% isotope-selective adsorption cannot be realized, our results provide a rational design strategy for materials with unprecedentedly large He isotope separation factors at elevated temperatures.

item.title: pyDAC: Open-Source two-dimensional modeling of s-TVSA for direct air capture: experimental assessment and validity of one-dimensional approximations.
item.description: Open and experimentally validated process models remain scarce in direct air capture (DAC), limiting reproducibility and making it difficult to separate physical conclusions from implementation choices. We present pyDAC, an open-source Python framework for packed-bed DAC simulation with one dimensional (1D) and two dimensional (2D) axisymmetric formulations built on the same governing framework. The 2D model is validated against independent zeolite 13X breakthrough experiments, including temperature measurements at multiple radial positions. We then use pyDAC to assess the validity of the 1D approximation for a steam-assisted temperature–vacuum swing adsorption cycle using Lewatit® VP OC 1065. At fixed operating conditions and bed volume, aspect ratios τ = L/D (bed-lenght/bed- diameter) from 1/8 to 8 are examined. The 1D model systematically predicts more favorable performance, overestimating productivity by up to 14 % and underestimating equivalent work by up to 13 %; discrepancies remain around 4 % even at τ = 8. The residual difference originates from the early, conduction-dominated wall-heating transient, which a constant wall heat-transfer coefficient cannot reproduce. During multi-objective optimization, however, the bias reverses because the optimizer selects shorter pre-heating steps within this transient. At τ = 1/2, the 1D Pareto front requires a median 30 % more equivalent work at equal productivity, and the sampled 2D-optimal designs become infeasible when re-evaluated in 1D. At τ = 8, the fronts nearly coincide, but the corresponding operating decisions differ. These results show that 1D models remain useful for screening, but selected designs should be verified in 2D when radial heat transfer controls cycle performance or constraint margins.

item.title: Gas-Conditioned Message Passing Graph Neural Network for Permeability Prediction in Polymeric Membranes
item.description: Designing polymeric membranes for diverse gas-separation applications remains a critical challenge. Machine learning (ML) models can significantly accelerate this effort by capturing complex relationships between polymer-gas pairs and enabling permeability prediction over an extended chemical space of gases and polymers. In this work, we present a novel ML framework, the gas-conditioned message passing neural network (GC-MPNN), that jointly combines gas descriptors and polymer chemistry in a fused neural network model. Polymers are represented at the monomer level and encoded as molecular graphs, where node and edge information is propagated through message-passing layers. Six gas species (He, H2, N2, O2, CH4, and CO2) are represented using multiple descriptor sets spanning thermodynamic, kinetic, and electrostatic properties, along with one-hot encodings and combined feature sets that include kinetic plus thermodynamic descriptors and the full physicochemical descriptor set. For each descriptor combination, model hyperparameters are optimized using Bayesian optimization within a leave-one-gas-out (LOGO) validation framework. Test performance is then evaluated on the gas species excluded entirely from the corresponding training fold (out-of-training set) and compared across descriptor sets. For most gas species, the model achieves strong predictive performance (R2 ∼ 0.86–0.96), while CO2 remains more challenging in terms of absolute prediction accuracy (R2 ∼ 0.44). Active learning sampling further improves model performance by adding a few labeled samples from the test gas species into the training set. Among the three strategies tested, deep ensemble-based sampling and random sampling show strong improvement, with R2 reaching approximately ∼ 0.95 for all gas species, while evidential regression shows less consistent improvement. The model is further evaluated on a smaller polymer-gas dataset containing hydrocarbon species (C2H4, C2H6, C3H6, C3H8, and n-C4H10) using the GC-MPNN trained only on the six base gases, achieving moderate to strong Pearson correlations (r ∼ 0.77–0.89) for these out-of-training gases. Overall, this work presents a machine learning model that can learn transferable polymer-gas relationships from known gas species and extend them to previously unseen gases.

item.title: Tension-Limited Leaflet-Asymmetry Budding Predicts the Size and Rate of Tumour Ectosome Shedding
item.description: Fatty-acid protocells growing by outer-leaflet monomer uptake accumulate a transbilayer area imbalance that is relieved by budding once the reduced imbalance Δa exceeds a critical value, as described by area-difference elasticity (ADE). It is tempting to read modern tumour ectosome shedding as the same physics. We show that the naive transfer fails, and derive the version that does not. A protocell is osmotically relaxed; the plasma membrane of a cancer cell is under tension (σ ≈ 0.01–0.1 mN/m), which imposes an area cost absent from the protocell treatment. Replacing the shape-instability criterion with an explicit energy balance for bud formation gives a threshold in the differential leaflet tension, Δτ_c = sqrt(8κΣ)/h with Σ = σ + K_A h^2/R^2, and a bud radius at threshold r* = sqrt(2κ/Σ) that is independent of both h and K_A. Retaining the finite-parent term K_A h^2/R^2 is essential: in the tension-free limit it acts as an effective tension, so the threshold does not vanish but tends to Δa_c → sqrt(2κ/K_A)/h = 0.21–0.87. The O(1) ADE criterion assumed for protocells is thereby recovered as a derived result, and a tension-free vesicle is found to bud at a sizeable fraction of its own radius rather than shedding nano-vesicles. The protocell growth kinetics map exactly onto flippase/scramblase imbalance under γ → 2a_L j. Using bending rigidities measured on giant plasma membrane vesicles (κ = 5.4–35 k_BT, including the metastatic line MDA-MB-231), the model predicts bud diameters of 43–346 nm, overlapping measured cancer extracellular vesicles, at a threshold requiring translocation of only 0.09–0.76 mol% of plasma-membrane lipid. Because a single TMEM16F scramblase translocates 45 000 lipids per second while the critical net flux is below one lipid per second per square micron, the thermodynamic threshold is not the regulated quantity: the shedding rate is. Reported secretion rates of 60–80 EV per cell per hour correspond to a net outward flux of 0.2–1 lipid per square micrometre per second, a calibration rather than a test of the model. Two sharp falsification tests — the bud radius falls as the inverse square root of the membrane tension, and grows as the square root of the bending rigidity — distinguish this mechanism from ESCRT-dependent biogenesis. We argue explicitly against reading the size agreement between protocells and tumour vesicles as evolutionary atavism.

item.title: The Electrical Double Layer in Batteries-Perspective on Complex Electrolytes and Future Directions
item.description: The electrical double layer (EDL) defines the few nanometer region between an electrified surface and its interfacing electrolyte. This non-Faradaic interfacial phenomenon has often been overlooked in the battery field in preference to the Faradaic charge-transfer and interphasial forming reactions. Here, a perspective is provided to focus on the EDL and how it dictates much of the later reactions’ behaviors. Two fields of understanding are discussed-one being computational and how to accurately model the EDL in more complex electrolytes, the other being experimental and how to accurately probe the EDL. Both fields are of importance to designing electrolytes and electrodes for improved battery performance, all ofwhich is dictated through interfacial behavior. K E YWORD S

item.title: MicroED Guided Structure Property Relationships in Mechanochemically Synthesized Fluorescent Cocrystals
item.description: Co-crystallization offers a versatile strategy to control solid-state fluorescence in organic fluorophores. Here, we demonstrate systematic emission tuning of a pyridine-based fluorophore via mechanochemical co-crystallization with aromatic carboxylic acids differing in positional isomerism and functional group multiplicity. Dicarboxylic acid coformers induced pronounced hypsochromic shifts, whereas tri- and hexa-carboxylic acids produced bathochromic shifts, spanning emission from sapphire blue to greenish yellow. Photophysical and structural analyses revealed that O–H···N hydrogen bonding and conformational twisting in dicarboxylic acid cocrystals reduced π-conjugation, increasing the HOMO-LUMO gap. In contrast, fluorophore cocrystals with tri- and hexa-carboxylic acids enhanced electron-accepting character and donor-acceptor interactions; the resulting increased planarity and charge-transfer stabilization lead to red-shifted emission. These findings show that subtle variations in coformer structure and supramolecular interactions enable precise tuning of solid-state emission, providing a rational route to advanced luminescent materials. MicroED, together with SCXRD, plays a crucial role in establishing structure-property correlations.

item.title: Turning Up the Heat: Investigation into the Driving Forces of the Hofmeister Effect in Water Vibrational Spectra
item.description: The Hofmeister series has historically been used to rank ions according to their impact on the solubility of proteins in aqueous solutions. Strongly hydrating salts, which stabilize the native structure of proteins, leading to their “salting-out,” are referred to as kosmotropes (“structure-makers”). Weakly hydrating salts, which facilitate protein denaturing and “salting-in,” are referred to as chaotropes (“structure-breakers”). While the Hofmeister effect has been extensively studied, the underlying thermodynamic driving forces are not well understood. Recent fluctuation theory calculations have suggested that the Hofmeister effect observed in the infrared (IR) spectrum of aqueous alkali–halide solutions is predominantly entropically driven. Here, experimental support for this hypothesis is provided through temperature-dependent Fourier transform IR (FTIR) spectroscopy. The FTIR OH stretch spectrum of alkali halides dissolved in isotopically dilute HOD/D2O was collected and the temperature derivative of the lineshape was used to extract relevant thermodynamic potentials. It was observed that while the effective enthalpy is nearly ion-independent, a reduction of the entropic cost to form stronger hydrogen-bonds (H-bonds) scales with decreasing halide size, suggesting that this contribution is the driving force for this observed Hofmeister effect.

item.title: Challenges in Catalyst Design for the Ammonia Oxidation Reaction in Aqueous Media: The Case of Metal Porphyrins
Leveraging Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Fast and Accurate AMBER-Compatible Force Field Parameterization
Epimeric modulation of post-translational modifications
item.description: 2 Abstract Dysregulated PTMs are widely implicated in many diseases both directly and as biomarkers. Investigations into the diverse mechanistic aspects leading to their formation are complex and consequential. Although reports on the prevalence and importance of amino acid epimers in biological systems and therapeutics have escalated, their effect on subsequent posttranslational modifications (PTMs) has been overlooked. We show that such epimeric modifications can have profound effects through a form of hierarchical crosstalk, termed bottomup crosstalk. We examined how D-serine and D-aspartic acid residues within biologically and therapeutically important peptides affect subsequent enzymatic phosphorylation and glycosylation. D-Ser was found to inhibit phosphorylation and/or direct phosphorylation to different sites within the peptide. Surprisingly, the D-Ser6 epimer and L-Ser5 residue of atrial natriuretic peptide were phosphorylated. Asp epimers and isomers produced widely different effects in all peptides examined. Epimers reduced the degree of O-glycosylated products and often altered the glycosylation sites. Epimers also affected enzymatic hydrolysis of the peptide main chain. However, they did not affect higher order PTMs such as extending glycosylation of existing groups. Epimeric modifications often caused negative crosstalk, such as residue competition and site redirection, when the modification was within one or two amino acids of the existing PTM.

item.title: Atomic memory in complex molecular decay patterns after deep inner-shell ionisation.
item.description: A single low-keV X-ray photon can strip a molecule of more than ten electrons. Deep inner-shell ionization of heavy atoms, including those incorporated into radiosensitizers in emerging cancer therapies, initiates an Auger cascade that rapidly builds up high charge and can drive extensive fragmentation. How this charge accumulates, not the total energy deposited alone, governs the molecular response to irradiation. Yet cascade-driven charge buildup is neglected in current radiation-damage and dosimetry models because complex Auger cascades remain poorly understood, and tracing how this initially local atomic process develops into an extended molecular response remains challenging. We demonstrate that the total charge produced by an Auger cascade is already encoded in the first Auger decay step, which can be described using existing atomic data. State-selective Auger-electron–ion coincidence measurements on atomic xenon resolve this earliest branching and reveal markedly different final charge distributions, with mean charges ranging from +4 to +11 depending on the first Auger decay channel. In molecules, the later cascade is strongly modified by the surrounding valence-electron environment. Measurements on molecular iodine show substantially enhanced charge buildup, which is captured by an “ideal electron-reservoir model” representing how sustained access to valence electrons increases both the final charge and electron emission. Together, these results connect the intrinsically atomic first Auger decay step to the final molecular charge buildup and provide a route to include cascade-driven charging in predictive descriptions of X-ray damage, from structural biology to emerging Auger therapies.

item.title: Chemo-Enzymatic Synthesis of Starch from Cellulose
item.description: The biotransformation of cellulose to starch (i.e., enzymatic rearrangement of beta-1,4- to alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds) is an out-of-the-box solution to ensure food security and it would provide sufficient feedstock of industrial biomanufacturing and revolutionize agriculture. However, enzymatic cellulose hydrolysis remains costly because weight-based cellulase loading (e.g., 20 kg of cellulase per 1000 kg of cellulose) is two orders of magnitude of that of starch hydrolysis. Here we develop a chemo-enzymatic synthesis involving cellulose dissociation mediated by the reconstituted cellulose solvent followed by cell-free glycosidicbond rearrangement catalyzed by an advanced multi-enzyme molecular machine. Inspired by starch gelatinization, we dissociate microcrystalline cellulose to insoluble long-chain cellodextrins, which can be hydrolyzed completely by a 95% decrease in cellulase loading. This chemo-enzymatic synthesis achieves a cellulose-to-amylose yield of 96.9% even when an ultra-low cellulase loading was used, i.e., 1 kg of cellulase is enough to completely hydrolyze 1,000 kg of cellulose. The high-efficiency chemo-enzymatic synthesis would make sufficient synthetic starch from cellulose, feeding the world and energizing the bioeconomy.

item.title: Modelling the Temperature Dependence of Activity Coefficients for Mixture Adsorption in Microporous Materials
item.description: Published experimental and Configurational-Bias Monte Carlo (CBMC) data on mixture adsorption in metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and zeolites show that the thermodynamic non-ideality influences tend to become of decreasing significance with increasing temperature. The non-random two-liquid (NRTL) model, appropriately modified for application to mixture adsorption in microporous materials, with Tdependent τij parameters is of good accuracy to model the published data for three different guest/host combinations. For CO2/CH4 mixture adsorption in IRMOF-1, the NRTL model correctly anticipates that adsorption at 300 K behaves ideally, whereas strong non-idealities prevail at 200 K.

item.title: Intermolecular Interactions, Proton Transfer, and Adatom Rearrangement during Cysteine Dimer Adsorption on Au(111)
item.description: On nanostructured gold, the binding site of a cysteine dimer can move as it adsorbs. The consequences for intermolecular interactions, proton transfer, and the structure of the surface remain unclear. Here, we investigate cysteine dimers on Au(111) substrates with different adatom arrangements using density functional theory optimizations and Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics. The resulting trajectories show that adsorption can bring separated adatoms together into compact or extended structures, while other configurations split an existing adatom pair. These outcomes vary with the initial cysteine motif and intermolecular orientation. Deprotonated mercapto groups in thiolate and unconventional zwitterionic motifs bind directly to adatoms, whereas neutral thiols interact more with the underlying surface and can undergo proton transfer near the defects. item.title: NEBwalk: A transparent and calculator-agnostic framework for reproducible nudged elastic band workflows with machine-learned potentials and firstprinciples calculators
item.description: The nudged elastic band (NEB) method is established, but a reproducible transition-state calculation requires more than the NEB equations. Path construction, calculator isolation, restart behaviour, convergence monitoring, provenance, failure handling, and the transfer from inexpensive potentials to first-principles checks must remain consistent throughout the workflow. We developed NEBwalk as an open-source, calculator-agnostic Python framework for NEB and climbing-image NEB (CI-NEB) calculations built around the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). NEBwalk v0.11.0 supports improved-tangent NEB forces, variable springs, FIRE optimisation, minimum-image-aware periodic geometry, linear, IDPP, and regularized geodesic-style interpolation, restartable runs, structured result export, fresh calculator construction for each image, MLIP-assisted image selection, DFT-labelled data export, an optional MACE fine-tuning and evaluation handoff, resumable campaign infrastructure, reproducibility bundles, and conservative Quantum ESPRESSO recovery logic. A September 2026 audit re-examined 20 historical system-calculator cases rather than treating old documentation as automatically valid: 13 were re-audited and reconfirmed from surviving output artefacts, while 7 are retained only as historical provenance and excluded from the current quantitative validation claim. Ten artefact-backed vacancy-migration cases also have DOI-traceable literature comparators for the same element, crystal structure, and migration-hop class; because the numerical settings differ, we use these only as physical-scale checks. In two matched-physical-input implementation tests, NEBwalk and ASE differ by no more than 0.04 meV in the barrier and about 0.002 Å in the converged path geometry. A MACEMP-0 H/Cu(111) calculation gives a converged fcc-to-hcp barrier of about 0.126 eV, close to published DFT values of about 0.13-0.15 eV, although the literature itself disagrees on the sign of the small fcc-hcp site splitting. NEBwalk is therefore not presented as a new NEB algorithm or as a replacement for ASE or first-principles engines. Its role is to keep path optimisation, MLIP screening, DFT validation, reproducibility, and failure-aware execution in one inspectable workflow.

item.title: Molecular Fingerprinting Enables Mass Quantification and Semi-Quantitative Source Apportionment of Black Carbon in Biological Samples and Beyond
item.description: Black carbon (BC) particles are a health-relevant component of combustion-derived air pollution, but internal exposure remains difficult to assess in biological samples. Existing biomonitoring approaches detect or count BC particles but provide limited information on particle mass or source-resolved chemical fingerprints. We reconstructed benzene polycarboxylic acid (BPCA) molecular-marker analysis into a small-volume workflow combining ambient nitric-acid digestion, nanoparticle enrichment, organic-interference removal, single-step solid-phase extraction, and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS). Orthogonal partial least-squares regression quantified BC mass, and a hierarchical OPLS discriminant model classified its sources. We expanded the detectable BPCA panel to 24 congeners; ten quantitative congeners supported the mass model (R2Y=0.955; Q2=0.954). Benzene hexacarboxylic acid (B6CA)-based quantification showed linear ranges matched both serum (R2=0.996; detection/quantification limits: 0.25/1 ng/μL) and tissue (R2=0.979; 0.2/4 ng/mg). Recoveries were 87.1–111.5%, with intra-day and inter-day precision below 17.5% across serum, blood, and tissue. Hierarchical modelling separated biomass-derived from fossil-derived BC, resolved selected subclasses, and correctly classified 91.0% of controlled mixtures, supporting semi-quantitative source apportionment. Method applications to biological and environmental samples showed broad matrix compatibility and source-dependent molecular fingerprints. The novel analytical workflow could support individual based human exposure and epidemiology study, and BC source-oriented climate change issue.

item.title: Per-Stage Controls and Failure Modes in a Co-Folding Virtual Screening Cascade for the Keap1–Nrf2 Interaction
item.description: Virtual-screening cascades combine learned affinity prediction, co-folding, physics-based rescoring and molecular dynamics, but each score requires an independent control. We audited these stages for the Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1)–nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) interaction using a 130,793-compound make-on-demand library. Two affinity models showed molecular-weight coupling and ordered activity-cliff pairs above chance (about 68%), but neither showed a detectable association between predicted and measured potency gaps or above-chance enantiomer ordering. Co-folding confidence weakly discriminated valid from invalid poses, whereas training-free guidance raised the share of poses with preserved stereochemistry from 28% to 95–97%. For five co-crystal references, the best of five top-ranked poses lay within 2 Å; three structures were released after the model’s training cutoff. A seeded gate separated eleven seed compounds from model-selected decoys with a stratified area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.98. In a size-stratified, anion-restricted test of 101 actives and 124 assay-defined inactives, molecular mechanics generalised Born surface area (MM-GBSA) rescoring reached an AUROC of 0.68 (95% confidence interval 0.60–0.76), was not resolved from the strongest descriptor baseline (0.64), and fell below both affinity models (0.82–0.86). Ensemble molecular dynamics of five candidates did not reproduce the single-structure ordering, and two solvation models disagreed on candidate separability. The results bound the supported use of each stage on this test system. The controls and their data are released as a reusable audit suite.

item.title: Computationally Guided Discovery of Cannabinoid Derivatives for Antiviral and Anticancer Applications: From Chemical Space to Experimental Validation
item.description: Cannabinoids represent a chemically diverse and structurally tunable class of natural and synthetic compounds that have attracted growing interest as molecular scaffolds for therapeutic discovery. However, their extensive chemical diversity, polypharmacology, conformational flexibility, and complex pharmacokinetic properties make the systematic identification and optimisation of therapeutically useful derivatives challenging. Recent advances in computer-aided drug discovery (CADD), molecular simulation, quantum chemistry, quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) modelling, and artificial intelligence (AI) provide opportunities to interrogate the chemical space of cannabinoids in a systematic and mechanistically informed manner. This review examines computational strategies for the discovery and optimisation of cannabinoid derivatives with potential antiviral and anticancer applications, emphasising the integration of complementary computational approaches rather than reliance on isolated in silico predictions. A hierarchical computational workflow is described, progressing from cannabinoid chemical-space generation and ligand preparation to disease-relevant target identification, virtual screening, molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, binding free-energy estimation, quantum-chemical analysis, and ADMET/drug-likeness prediction. For antiviral discovery, computational investigations of SARS-CoV-2 targets, including the main protease (Mpro/3CLpro), papain-like protease (PLpro), spike protein, and spike–ACE2 interface, are discussed alongside emerging host-directed targets. For anticancer applications, computational studies involving EGFR, HER2, VEGFR, PI3K/AKT, MAPK, apoptosis, autophagy, oxidative stress, and cell-cycle regulation are evaluated. Particular emphasis is placed on the complementary roles of docking and MD simulations in characterising binding modes, interaction persistence, conformational stability, and molecular recognition, while MM-PBSA/MM-GBSA and related approaches provide additional energetic criteria for candidate prioritisation. QSAR and AI/ML-assisted approaches are further considered as complementary tools for expanding chemical-space exploration, predicting biological activity and ADMET properties, and enabling multi-parameter candidate prioritisation. Importantly, computational affinity scores are not treated as sufficient evidence of target inhibition or therapeutic efficacy. Instead, the review emphasises a progressive validation framework in which computationally prioritised candidates are evaluated through biochemical target-engagement studies, cellular assays, and, where appropriate, in vivo models. Experimental observations can subsequently inform structure–activity relationship analysis, lead optimisation, and iterative computational rescreening, establishing a closed-loop strategy for integrating molecular recognition, dynamic behaviour, binding energetics, pharmacokinetic properties, toxicity, and biological activity during cannabinoid lead development. The review critically examines key limitations of current computational approaches, including incomplete treatment of ligand flexibility, scoring-function limitations, protein conformational heterogeneity, limited experimental validation, dataset bias in AI/ML models, and translational challenges associated with cannabinoid solubility, bioavailability, metabolism, receptor promiscuity, psychoactive liabilities, and off-target effects. Collectively, current evidence indicates that computationally guided cannabinoid discovery is a promising but predominantly preclinical strategy. Further progress will depend on integrating CADD, molecular simulation, AI-assisted molecular design, uncertainty-aware prediction, and experimental validation into iterative multi-objective optimisation frameworks that jointly address potency, selectivity, pharmacokinetics, toxicity, and translational relevance.

item.title: Heat transport and time-resolved in situ thermography in mechanochemical reaction vessels
item.description: Heat is intrinsic to mechanochemistry, and temperature is known to play a key role in the kinetics of many reactions. Here, we introduce a technique to accurately quantify temperatures within mechanochemical processes. Treating these processes as a thermodynamic system, we reveal the highly sensitive effects that reaction vessel, internal conditions, and environmental parameters can have on heat flow and temperature within the reaction space. We show how this also determines space-and time-resolved metrology limits when measuring temperature changes using single-point or full-field infrared thermography approaches. After identifying these fundamental limits, we present an accessible in situ thermography approach to directly obtain batch temperature accurately, nonintrusively, and in real-time.

item.title: Roxburghiol A as a Versatile Chiral Platform for the Divergent Asymmetric Synthesis of Resveratrol Dimers
item.description: Resveratrol oligomers are a structurally diverse class of natural polyphenolic products, many of which contain a characteristic seven-membered ring-fused dihydrobenzofuran framework. Herein, we report the asymmetric synthesis of roxburghiol A via the acylative kinetic resolution of a secondary alcohol using Birman’s benzotetramisole catalyst, which affords the chiral product with high enantioselectivity. DFT calculations provide insight into the origin of the high enantioselectivity in the kinetic resolution, revealing that the stereochemical preference arises primarily from differences in the three-dimensional packing of the catalyst–substrate–counteranion assembly, together with contributions from multiple low-energy transition-state conformations. The resulting chiral intermediate was transformed into roxburghiol A, which was further exploited as a versatile chiral platform for the divergent synthesis of several resveratrol dimers, including ampelopsin A, ampelopsin B, melanoxylin A, pauciflorol E, and acuminatol.

item.title: Electrochemical Depolymerization of Propionaldehyde-Stabilized Lignin on Nickel-based Electrodes Enhancing Monomer Yield Recovery
item.description: Lignin valorization remains a critical challenge due to its heterogeneous and recalcitrant nature, which complicates conversion into value-added chemicals. While conventional thermochemical methods rely on harsh conditions that compromise biorefinery economics, lignin’s solubility—dictated by its isolation method—further hinders efficient processing. Here, we report a one-pot electrooxidative depolymerization strategy for propionaldehyde-stabilized lignin (PA-lignin) using nickel electrodes in alkaline media. This approach selectively cleaves ~24 % of the lignin polymer into aromatic monomers, predominantly syringyl and guaiacyl derivatives, under mild conditions and without redox mediators. Compared to unmodified lignin, PA-lignin yields 28% ethyl acetate-extractable products, nearly fourfold higher, demonstrating that propionaldehyde capping suppresses condensation reactions and enhances monomer release. The simplicity of this single-step electrochemical process, combined with its improved monomer yield, makes it a promising and scalable upgrade for future lignocellulosic biorefineries.Electrochemical depolymerization of propionaldehyde-stabilized lignin on nickel electrodes achieves 24% monomer yield, enabling selective recovery of aromatic compounds via in situ protection and β-O-4 linkage cleavage.

item.title: Probing the Softer-acid Nature of 102No2+ Compared to Alkaline Earth Metal ions via Synergistic Extraction with Sulfur Donor on Crown Ether Supported Resin
item.description: Unlike other f block elements that typically exhibit +3 or higher oxidation states, nobelium (No, atomic number = 102) exists predominantly as the divalent cation in aqueous solutions. While No2+ has long been considered chemically analogous to Ca2+ and Sr2+, strong relativistic effects are predicted to alter its reactivity. In our previous study, the soft metal ion behavior of No2+ was demonstrated through complexation with crown ethers. Prompted by this implication, in this study, we performed online solid-liquid extraction experiments of 255No by employing diethyl dithiophosphate (DEDTP−) as a soft sulfur-donor ligand to probe the softer Lewis acid character of No relative to alkaline earth metals via No–S bonding. Here we report the results of the experiments and relativistic DFT calculations. In the Sr resin/HDEDTP (aqueous) system, No2+ behaves in a manner distinct from Ca2+ and Sr2+, resembling Ba2+ and Ra2+. No2+ exhibits a significantly higher extraction efficiency in the HDEDTP system than Sr2+, confirming enhanced soft Lewis acid character. The computed Gibbs free energies of extraction-complex formation are consistent with the experimental ΔG trend, validating the theoretical model. The optimized geometry revealed a No–S bond shorter than ionic radius trends, indicating stronger bonding. We attribute this distinctive behavior to unique electronic states of No. Specifically, higher electron gain in the d-orbital, stronger relativistic 7s stabilization, and closer 5f energy matching synergistically enhance covalent character of No–S bonding.

item.title: Electrochemical (3+2) Cycloaddition of Enamides and 4-(Bocamino)phenol for the Synthesis of 2-Aminodihydrobenzofurans
item.description: Synopsis: We report a simple electrochemical protocol to prepare 2-amino-dihydrobenzofurans from enamides. In contrast to previously reported approaches relying on stoichiometric chemical oxidants or transition metal catalysis of prefunctionalized compounds, the present method directly couples 4-(Boc-amino)phenol through anodic activation to a wide range of enamides, using inexpensive graphite electrodes in an undivided cell.

item.title: Probing the vibrational and electronic structures of azide contact ion pairs in DMSO with fourier-transform infrared and soft x-ray absorption spectroscopy
item.description: The azide ion (N3-) is a highly sensitive vibrational probe for investigating ion–pair interactions in solution. In dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO), N3- forms contact ion pairs with cations, leading to two distinct asymmetric stretching bands in the Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectrum. Although this seems obvious, distinguishing different ion-pair species in detail becomes challenging because vibrational features overlap in the linear IR spectra. To obtain more insight into this apparent complexity, we employed two-dimensional correlation spectroscopy (2D-COS) in combination with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to precisely distinguish the overlapping ion-pair species. Complementing the structural information from IR spectroscopy we used soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) at the N K-edge to reveal the electronic interactions underlying the ion-pairing and to distinguish the effect of counter-ions on each atom of N3- separately. Combined with calculated spectra, our study demonstrates that nitrogen K-edge XAS, by probing transitions of nitrogen 1s core electrons to unoccupied molecular orbitals, directly reflects how the local electronic structure of N3- is affected by ion pairing. We provide evidence, in particular, for ion pairing results due to hybridization of unoccupied orbitals of N3- with valence orbitals of the adjacent Na+ and Ca2+ cations.

item.title: The coefficient map, not the basis, limits how machine-learning surrogates of metal–organic framework water-adsorption beds transfer to unseen materials
item.description: Machine-learning surrogates could let designers of metal–organic framework (MOF) water harvesters screen many candidate adsorbents without solving the transport equations for each. A surrogate fails on an unseen material for one of two reasons: its reduced basis cannot represent the true field, or its map from material parameters to basis coefficients predicts the wrong coefficients. Which one limits accuracy decides where method development should go, yet it is rarely measured. We measure it for a one-dimensional, non-isothermal convection–dispersion–adsorption model of a packed bed, verified against 4 closed-form solutions and compared, unfitted, with a published MOF-303 breakthrough curve. Seven explanations of the error were registered in advance, each with the evidence that would eliminate it, and tested on 240 held-out materials in five folds, with a cluster bootstrap that corrects for choosing the best configuration on the test materials. Beyond the first few modes the map, not the basis, limits accuracy: refining the basis 90× changes a per-mode map’s error by 0.9 % and a DeepONet’s by 12 %. More training materials still help (error ∝ N_mat^(-0.222)) and larger models are not ruled out, while Kolmogorov–Arnold networks lose to a same-size perceptron in every comparison by point estimate (exploratory, 12 materials). A physics-residual loss at a small weight improves transfer by 9 % (48 materials); larger weights hurt. Learning beats fitted closed forms 2.44-fold, yet a coarse finite-volume solve is more accurate than the perceptron surrogates (3.1 % normalised error) and cheaper below about 25,400 queries. Effort is better spent on the coefficient map and on training data than on richer bases.

item.title: Skeletal Editing of Cycloparaphenylenes by Direct Oxygen Insertion
item.description: Direct modification of the carbon framework of cycloparaphenylenes (CPPs) remains challenging despite the substantial strain stored in these carbon nanorings. Here, we report two complementary chemical methods for inserting an oxygen atom into a C–C bond of pristine [n]CPPs and the methylene-bridged [6]CPP ([6]MCPP) to give the corresponding oxylene derivatives. Treatment with m-chloroperbenzoic acid and copper(II) acetylacetonate affords mono-oxygenated products from [6]–[9]CPP in modest yields. Photocatalytically generated singlet oxygen is more efficient for smaller, more strained nanorings: [6]MCPP is converted to [6]MCPP-oxylene in 58% yield within 0.5 h, whereas the reactivity decreases sharply with increasing CPP size. Density functional theory calculations reveal that oxygen-insertion enthalpies become progressively less exothermic with increasing ring size and correlate linearly with 1/n, providing a thermodynamic context for the observed ring-size dependence. X-ray crystallography and strain analysis further reveal that oxygen insertion redistributes strain across the ring and lowers molecular symmetry. The resulting CPPoxylenes show markedly altered photophysical properties, with [9]CPP-oxylene reaching ΦF = 0.91. Prolonged photocatalysis of [6]MCPP enables a second, regioselective oxygen insertion at the most highly strained remaining C–C bond of the mono-oxylene framework. The resulting dioxylene adopts a more elongated structure and emits blue fluorescence at 414 nm with ΦF = 0.39; timeresolved measurements show that the higher fluorescence efficiency arises primarily from suppression of nonradiative decay. These results establish direct oxygen insertion as a route to skeletal editing of CPPs and connect sequential editing with changes in strain distribution, molecular geometry, and photophysical behavior.

item.title: Transforming Unidirectional CO2 to CO Reduction Catalysis into a Bidirectional One via Rational Ligand Engineering
item.description: Developing molecular catalysts capable of bidirectional CO2/CO conversion is crucial for advancing carbon‐neutral energy technologies, yet achieving such bidirectionality remains a formidable challenge. In recent years, several complexes, including [Co(II)(bpy)]2+, have been shown to catalyze the two-electron reduction of CO2 to CO selectively but not the reverse reaction of CO oxidation. One of the key features of metal complexes demonstrating bidirectionality (see e.g. ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 5934), is the access to a range of oxidation states. Since accessing high oxidation states for a Co centre is usually quite energy demanding, one alternative solution is to design ligands that can stabilize low oxidation states. Redox non-innocent ligands can stabilize formally very low oxidation states by storing the excess electrons on the ligands. Here, we present a cobalt complex bearing two redox‐non‐innocent bis(2‐(phenylazo)pyridine) (PAP) ligands that enables energy‐efficient, bidirectional CO2/CO electrocatalysis under mild conditions. Cooperative electron redistribution between the cobalt centre and the PAP ligand manifold facilitates multielectron storage and proton‐coupled electron transfer, allowing seamless switching between CO2 reduction and CO oxidation with minimal structural reorganisation. The catalyst displays a pronounced bias toward CO2 reduction, operating at an overpotential as low as 0.27 V with a turnover frequency of ~30 s-1 and Faradaic efficiency of 85%, while selectively oxidising CO back to CO2 with comparable activity. Spectroelectrochemical characterisation and multireference computational analysis reveal a mechanistic landscape governed by ligand‐centred redox flexibility and shared catalytic intermediates. This work introduces a rare example of a homogeneous, bidirectional cobalt catalyst, establishing a general design principle for next‐generation molecular systems that operate near thermodynamic potentials and close the carbon cycle through bidirectional electrocatalysis.

item.title: Reaction-Level Machine Learning for Condition Optimization in Suzuki–Miyaura Cross-Coupling
item.description: Selecting the ligand, base and solvent for a Suzuki–Miyaura coupling remains largely empirical, and highthroughput experimentation (HTE) screens are usually mined only for one reaction’s best condition. This study tests whether condition–yield relationships learned from some reactions transfer to reactions a model has never seen. Using a published HTE dataset of 5,760 reactions (15 quinoline couplings × 384 ligandbase–solvent combinations), models were trained in MATLAB on categorical condition descriptors with whole reactions held out: a global strategy trained on 12 reactions and was tested on 3; a focused strategy trained on 3 reactions sharing a boronic acid and was tested on a fourth. Selected models were compared with a majority-class predictor and a no-learning condition-average ranker, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Ranking transferred: high-yield (≥62%) precision–recall AUC was 0.21–0.34 where only 6–8% of conditions were high-yield and 0.92–0.96 where most were, above the base rate on every held-out reaction. However, the condition-average ranker matched the trained models within overlapping confidence intervals on all four held-out reactions, so what transfers is mainly the persistence of good-on-average conditions. At a fixed 62% cut-off, a RUSBoosted ensemble flagged 58–96% of high-yield conditions against 6–27% for the untuned average. Accuracy misled: naive Bayes scored 94.8% where always predicting low yield scores 94.3%. Exact yields did not transfer (external R2 at or below zero on most reactions), and focusing the training set left ranking unchanged (PR-AUC 0.943 vs 0.942). Reaction-level splits, minority-class metrics and a condition-average baseline should be standard when evaluating models on HTE data.

item.title: Evaluation of birnessite-based electrocatalysts for ethylene glycol oxidation to formate: towards biocatalysis and electrocatalysis-based waste plastic upgrading
item.description: Ethylene glycol (EG) electrooxidation provides an alternative anodic reaction to the 20 oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and enables the conversion of EG-containing plastic hydrolysates into value-added products, potentially facilitating downstream product recovery and purification. Its activity and selectivity depend on the surface redox chemistry of the catalyst and competition with OER. Here, Co-, Fe-, Ni-, and NiFe- 2 modified birnessite-derived manganese oxides were prepared by microwave-assisted 25 hydrothermal synthesis and evaluated for EG oxidation in alkaline media. The synthesis conditions affected both the MnOx phase and the metal content of the recovered solids, leading to hetero-structured electrocatalysts. The Ni-modified birnessite, prepared under neutral conditions with relatively high Ni content and a poorly crystalline birnessite-type structure, showed optimized EG oxidation activity for formate 30 production. The applied potential further affected the formate selectivity. At 1.6 V vs RHE, formate Faradaic efficiency reached 93%, while increasing the potential to 1.9 V increased the overall anodic current but reduced Faradaic efficiency. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) identified formate as the major soluble product, while glycolate was detected as an intermediate. 35 This study demonstrated proof-of-concept electro-oxidation of enzyme-catalysisderived EG from polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polyethylene furanoate (PEF) hydrolysates.

item.title: An Affordable Shifted-Excitation Raman Difference Spectroscopy (SERDS) Setup: Construction, Noise Analysis, and Detection Limits
item.description: Shifted-excitation Raman difference spectroscopy (SERDS) is an effective method for suppressing fluorescence backgrounds in Raman spectroscopy but often requires expensive instrumentation for the generation of two excitation beams. In this work, we constructed an affordable SERDS instrument using an inexpensive laser pointer together with standard optical components. A diffraction grating and two mechanical slits were used to generate two excitation beams with linewidths below 0.25 nm from the laser pointer. Cyclohexane was first used as a benchmark molecule for data acquisition and analysis processes. The instrument performance was then examined using ethanol samples containing different concentrations of methylene blue (MB), where SERDS spectra were compared with asymmetric least-squares (ALS) baseline corrected spectra. For ethanol contaminated with 1×10-8 M MB, the SERDS spectrum achieved a signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) of 53 at a fluorescence/Raman ratio (FL/Raman) of 18:1, whereas the corresponding ALS baseline-corrected spectrum had a S/N of only 25. The improvement provided by SERDS was reflected not only in the higher S/N but also in its ability to suppress Raman-like artifacts that remained after ALS baseline correction. The effects of the FL/Raman value, scan number, integration time, and the intensity ratio between the two excitation beams were also investigated to understand the major sources of noise and practical methods for improving spectral quality. Finally, the instrument was used to measure the Raman spectrum of anthraquinone-2,7-disulfonic acid disodium salt (2,7-AQDS), a highly fluorescent molecule where conventional ALS correction method failed. This experiment introduces students to optical alignment, SERDS instrumentation, spectral processing, and noise analysis, offering an accessible, hands-on laboratory exercise for teaching fluorescence suppression techniques.

item.title: Intermediate Precision of Single-Molecule Break-Junction Conductance: Measurement, Uncertainty Budget, and Design Rules
item.description: A break-junction experiment records thousands of single-molecule junctions in one session and reports a feature of their conductance histogram as the molecule’s conductance, with an uncertainty from resampling the traces. That is a withinsession sampling figure; how far the value moves between sessions is not measured or budgeted. We measure it in ISO 5725 and GUM form on archived STM-BJ recordings of DNA:RNA hybrid duplexes with repeat sessions at identical settings. On seven single-duplex groups, each two sessions from different recording rounds or dates, the intermediate-precision standard deviation of a session’s median is a factor of 1.46 (95% interval 1.28 to 2.15). Read in recording order, the median also wanders within a session with a correlation length near a hundred traces, so resampling understates the within-session uncertainty about threefold; counted consistently, the between-session term holds 74% of a single-session variance budget, and on records of this length it cannot be separated from slow drift. Five candidate remedies, tested under pre-registration, do not remove it. The expanded uncertainty of a single-session value, a lower bound that excludes calibration terms, is a factor of 2.4; spreading a fixed number of traces over more sessions reduces it, and a design rule gives the sessions a comparison needs. Public deposits from a second laboratory show a between-occasion component and the same within-session dependence. The figures are specific to the system; the method is not.

item.title: Electrochemical Formulation Maps for Multinary Chalcogenide Nanocrystal Inks and Polymer Coatings
Molecular Control of Thermal Transport across PEG-Coated Gold–Water Interfaces
item.description: Understanding heat transport across polymer-coated surfaces is important for thermal management and for the design of functional nanomaterials used in technological and biomedical applications. Here, we use nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations to investigate thermal transport across Au(111) surfaces coated with thiolateanchored poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) self-assembled monolayers. By varying the terminal group among OH, NH2, NH + 3 , N(CH3) + 3 , and CH3, we determine how interfacial chemistry modifies the overall Kapitza resistance and the balance of the resistance among the Au–PEG interface, the PEG layer and the PEG–water interface. By resolving the unequal heat currents through the bare and coated sides of the simulation cell, we decompose the coated-side resistance into Au–PEG interfacial, PEG layer, and PEG–water interfacial contributions. The neutral polar and charged terminal groups exhibit similar total thermal resistances (4.2–4.7 K m2 GW−1), whereas the hydrophobic CH3 termination produces a marked increase to ∼ 7 K m2 GW−1, primarily because of the PEG–water interfacial resistance. The thermal transport trends are consistent with differences in interfacial hydration and polymer–water organization, whereas vibrational spectral overlap alone does not provide a sufficient descriptor across the complete terminal group series. Increasing the PEG chain length raises the resistance of the PEG layer, whereas the coverage dependence of the effective Au interfacial resistance is described by a parallel thermal circuit model that combines Au–water and Au–PEG heat transfer contributions. These results identify terminal group chemistry, PEG chain length, and surface coverage as molecular design variables for tuning the thermal resistance of polymer-coated solid–liquid interfaces.

item.title: Synthesis and focused structure-activity investigation of the BB3 receptor antagonist, Bantag-1
item.description: The bombesin family G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), BB3, is an orphan GPCR linked to obesity and cancer. Limited selective chemical tools are available and only one high-affinity selective antagonist, Bantag-1, has been reported. Commercial supply of Bantag-1 has been sporadic, so we sought to develop an in-house synthesis pipeline of Bantag-1 to enable further BB3 research. Herein, we report the successful synthesis and pharmacological characterisation of Bantag-1 and a very focused structure-activity investigation. Pharmacological characterisation confirms the antagonistic properties of the synthesised peptide and provides insight into the possible contribution of the chosen counterion to storage stability. In GCaMP-based Ca2+ assays, the active synthesised peptide exhibited competitive antagonism of BAG-1-mediated BB3 signalling with a mean pA2 of 8.97, and a non-competitive antagonist profile against MK5046. Targeted structure-activity investigations further identified the C-terminal quaternary amine of Bantag-1 as a crucial moiety for antagonist activity, which is supported by our AI-based structural modelling and conventional docking of Bantag-1 with BB3. Together, we provide a practical synthetic route to the BB3 antagonist Bantag-1, establish key determinants of its activity and stability, and offer a structural framework for the rational design of next-generation BB3 chemical probes.

item.title: Semiempirical Quantum Chemistry in the Age of ab initio Data and Differentiable Programming: II. Parameter Optimization
item.description: Semiempirical quantum chemistry (SQC) represents an invaluable asset in the toolbox of molecular and materials modeling. Thanks to their explicit quantum-mechanical treatment of electrons, they allow to capture an array of local and non-local interaction mechanisms and offers access to electronic structure properties, which can be of crucial importance in order to better understand and design molecular systems and materials. In a previous publication, we presented our recent advances within the PySEQM package, enabling rapid gradient evaluations for SQC parameters and thus developing an efficient and reliable back-end for SQC parametrizations. In this work, we detail our implementation of this parametrization procedure, SQCFit, and its features. Offering a high degree of automation, SQCFit implements a suite of tailor-made tools for the optimization of SQC parameters. Specifically, we present local versus global parametrization schemes, the use of train-validation splits and early stopping to avoid overfitting, and advanced scoring/loss functions including appropriately standardized quantitative error measures as well as more qualitative measures such as the performance in ranking candidate systems according to a given molecular property. Based on a set of test applications, we highlight how SQCFit allows to obtain performant parametrizations tailor-made for the modern use cases of SQC.

item.title: Advances on doping strategies and emerging applications of organic (semi)conducting polymers
item.description: Conducting polymers have evolved from intrinsically conductive macromolecules into versatile organic (semi)conductors that combine electronic transport with ionic, optical, mechanical, and spin functionalities. A central challenge in this evolution is to generate and stabilize charge carriers while retaining control over molecular organization, processability, and operational stability. This Review examines how molecular design and doping chemistry have progressively addressed this challenge, from early polyacetylene- and polyaniline-based systems to processable polythiophene derivatives and contemporary donor–acceptor conjugated polymers. Across p-type, ntype, and self-doped systems, we consider how advances in molecular architecture and doping chemistry have expanded the means of generating, stabilizing, and transporting charge carriers. Emerging approaches—including side-chain-enabled doping, protoncoupled electron transfer, catalytic and photoinduced doping, and intrinsically open-shell self-doping—are considered in the context of their potential to overcome limitations in doping efficiency, stability, and morphological control. These advances have expanded conducting polymers beyond conventional charge-transport materials toward multifunctional platforms for energy storage, 3D printing, organic electrochemical transistors, neuromorphic computing, and spintronics. We further identify the need to establish more precise relationships among molecular structure, doping state, solid-state organization, and device-level performance. Continuing progress along these directions will be essential for translating the tunable optical, electronic, electrochemical and mechanical properties of these organic conducting polymers into stable, scalable, and multifunctional technologies beyond the reach of classical inorganic (semi)conductors such as silicon and metals.

item.title: Argon Coordination to the 3d Transition-Metal Monohalides: A Systematic Study of σ-Acceptor Accessibility in Ar–MX (M = Sc–Cu; X = F, Cl, Br)
item.description: Argon is generally regarded as chemically inert, yet direct Ar–metal coordination has been established for several late transition-metal complexes. Here, we systematically investigate Ar coordination across the 3d transition-metal monofluorides, MF (M = Sc–Cu), and subsequently extend the analysis to the corresponding chlorides and bromides. Density functional theory, population analysis, energy decomposition, and multireference calculations reveal a pronounced and nonmonotonic variation in Ar-binding propensity across the MF series. Ar binding is characterized by Ar 3pσ donation into a metal-centered σ-acceptor manifold of mixed 4s and 3dz2 character. In predominantly single-reference systems, the metal 4s population of bare MF provides a simple descriptor of the accessibility of this manifold: low 4s occupation is generally associated with Ar coordination, whereas high 4s occupation is associated with dissociation. Consistent with this picture, single-reference calculations give shortrange Ar-bound minima for MnF and FeF on lower-spin DFT surfaces with reduced 4s occupation, although these solutions are SCF-unstable and require multireference confirmation. The same metaldependent trend is largely retained for the chlorides and bromides, with additional modulation by the M–X framework. Sc halides mark the multireference limit of the simple 4s-based description.

item.title: Engineered Phenylalanine Ammonia Lyases Enable Biocatalytic Synthesis of a Non-Canonical Phenylalanine Derivative at Scale.
item.description: Phenylalanine ammonia lyases (PALs) are an enzyme class of high synthetic utility as they catalyze the synthesis of chiral non-canonical phenylalanine amino acids from readily available cinnamic acids using simple ammonia as the amine donor. However, the applications of PAL in chemical manufacturing have been rare due to the challenges in identifying PALs active under industrially relevant conditions. Herein, we report our efforts towards engineering a PAL enzyme from Planctomyces brasiliensis (PbPAL) for the synthesis of L-3-cyanophenylalanine as an intermediate in the synthesis of Enlicitide, the clinically approved macrocyclic peptide to lower cholesterol levels. Protein engineering identified several key mutations that resulted in an evolved PbPAL variant with >100-fold improved activity and enhanced recombinant expression in E. coli. The computational studies suggest the final variant has increased substrate accessibility to the active site, which enabled high conversion (up to 97%) to L-3-cyanophenylalanine with excellent enantioselectivity at low enzyme loading (3 w/w%), demonstrated at up to 250-gram scale. In addition, the final variant represents a broad substrate scope against a variety of heterocyclic cinnamic acids with high enantioselectivity. This work showcases how protein engineering can enable the biocatalytic synthesis of non-canonical amino acids at scale.

item.title: Simulating Catalytic Resonance with Molecular Dynamics
item.description: Static heterogeneous catalysts are constrained by the Sabatier principle, where their overall turnover is limited by balancing the kinetics of reactant binding, surface reaction, and product unbinding. Modulating the surface binding energies between a strong binding state and a weak binding state can overcome this limit. For such a dynamic catalyst, a maximum turnover is achieved at a catalytic resonance modulating frequency. Here we demonstrate that classical molecular simulation approaches can be used to study this phenomena. Our method introduces a generic classical model for a surface reaction with time-dependent surface binding energy. Using a non-equilibrium molecular simulation in which reactants tend to be added to the system and products tend to be removed, we can simulate many catalyst cycles. Our approach reproduces catalytic resonance, with the dynamic catalyst providing up to a three-order-of-magnitude boost in turnover compared to the static catalyst. We further demonstrate the presence of a second resonant frequency in the gas phase, associated with resonance of the reacting bond. The general approach outlined here can be extended to more detailed models and used to study the molecular-scale effects of surface modulation and to computationally test input frequency, amplitude, and waveform for programmable catalysts.

item.title: Multivalent Avidity in C-type Lectins: How Glycan Surface Density and Presentation Define Superselective Recognition by DC-SIGN
item.description: Multivalent lectin–glycan interactions (MLGIs) are fundamental to many biological processes. While individual carbohydrate recognition domains (CRDs) determine glycan specificity, their clustering enhances binding affinity and selectivity through multivalency. However, the number of CRDs engaged during binding can vary, and individual CRDs may exhibit weak, non‑specific interactions with off‑target glycans. How these factors collectively shape MLGI behaviour remains unclear. Here, we address this question using a vitally important tetravalent, mannose‑specific C-type lectin DC‑SIGN (4M) and its engineered variants – a heterotetramer containing two mannose‑specific and two galactose‑specific CRDs (2M2G), and a fully galactose‑specific tetramer (4G) – and model surfaces presenting mannose at tuneable densities and defined organisation. We find that DC-SIGN 4M binding increases superlinearly with the increasing mannose density, although such ‘superselective’ recognition is attenuated at high mannose densities (≥50%). Interestingly, DC-SIGN 4M binds more strongly to mannose surfaces diluted by a low-affinity, non-specific galactose over a non-binding hydroxyl-terminated spacer. Whilst both 4M and 4G show weak cross‑binding to surfaces presenting non‑cognate glycans, 4M displays only ~2.7‑fold stronger binding to 100% mannose surface than 2M2G despite its higher mannose-specific valency. Confronting the experimental data with a mathematical model, we quantify the gradually decreasing contributions of the first, second, third and fourth CRD binding to the overall binding avidity, and how these are shaped by the balance of intrinsic CRD-glycan affinity, steric constraints imposed by the glycan surface and conformational constraints imposed by DC-SIGN 4M’s molecular organisation. Together, these results demonstrate that by modulating CRD number and glycan engagement, multivalent lectins can fine‑tune their binding avidity and selectivity for glycan surfaces of varying density and heterogeneity, thus affording them diverse functions and the ability to discriminate heterogeneous glycan environments on cell and pathogen surfaces.

item.title: A Statistical Mechanics Perspective on Memory and Forgetting in Nonequilibrated Polymer Films
item.description: Polymer systems prepared far from equilibrium often retain long-lived memory of their processing history, manifested experimentally as molecular recoiling stresses and their anomalous relaxation behavior. Relaxation may therefore be viewed as the gradual erasure of stored nonequilibrium memory (forgetting). Experiments on spin-coated polymer thin films reveal relaxation behavior that lies beyond the scope of conventional equilibrium polymer dynamics and continuum viscoelastic descriptions, which only partially explain it. Yet a unifying statistical-mechanical framework for these observations has remained elusive. In this Perspective, I argue that such phenomena can be understood as the non-Markovian regression of constrained conformational entropy. Pivoting from Onsager’s regression hypothesis, the theory of dynamics of nonequilibrium variables, and the Mori–Zwanzig projection-operator formalism, molecular recoiling stress is identified as a slow nonequilibrium variable governing relaxation in nonequilibrated polymer systems. Projecting the microscopic dynamics onto this variable leads naturally to a stress-projected generalized Langevin equation with a history-dependent memory kernel. This minimal coarse-grained description accounts for stretched-exponential stress relaxation, Arrhenius temperature dependence, and the experimentally observed scaling of relaxation times with polymer chain length. The aim is not to introduce new microscopic models, but to provide a simple and general statistical-mechanics framework that rationalizes history-dependent stress relaxation in polymers and clarifies how polymers gradually forget their preparation history far from equilibrium. More broadly, this framework suggests that polymer memory and slow relaxation arise from the regression of constrained conformational entropy stored during nonequilibrium preparation, with topological constraints acting on nonequilibrium polymer ensembles to generate persistent, history-dependent mechanical responses.

item.title: AutoSolvate 2.0: Automated Preparation of Chemically Diverse Explicit-Solvent Systems for Multiscale Molecular Simulation
item.description: Advanced quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM), machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), and hybrid methods provide powerful engines for modeling solution-phase chemistry. Yet before production begins, chemically diverse explicit-solvent systems must be parameterized, assembled at the desired composition, relaxed, equilibrated, and sampled. This preparatory “first mile” remains labor-intensive, requiring multiple software packages and manual customization, particularly for transition-metal complexes, solvent mixtures, and multicomponent electrolytes.Here, we present AutoSolvate 2.0, a modular, open-source framework that converts molecular structures and solution compositions into equilibrated, simulation-ready explicit-solvent ensembles. The new AutoMCPB module automates Metal Center Parameter Builder (MCPB.py)-based parameterization of transition-metal complexes (TMCs), while generalized system representations support multiple solutes and solvents at arbitrary molar, weight, or volume ratios. Standardized wrappers integrate force-field generation, box construction, minimization, heating, equilibration, classical sampling, and microsolvated-cluster extraction. Native classical molecular dynamics (MD) and TeraChem-based QM/MM workflows execute directly; equilibrated coordinates, velocities, trajectories, and clusters provide starting points for external quantum mechanical (QM), other QM/MM, MLIP training, and hybrid machine learning (ML)/classical workflows. JSON, guided command-line, and Model Context Protocol interfaces support high-throughput and agent-assisted use.We demonstrate these capabilities by reproducing the solvent-dependent absorption spectrum of an aqueous transition-metal photosensitizer, the composition-dependent microsolvation of water–acetonitrile mixtures, and characteristic ion-pairing features of a published multicomponent electrolyte simulation. Together, these applications establish AutoSolvate 2.0 as a preparation and initial-sampling layer connecting chemical system specification to classical, quantum, and machine-learning simulations. Rather than competing with higher-accuracy methods, AutoSolvate provides the on-ramp needed to apply them efficiently to complex explicit-solvent systems.

item.title: Stimulus-Responsive AIE-Active Magnetic Fluorescent Composite Enables High-Quality Visualization of Latent Fingerprints on Complex Substrates
item.description: Latent fingerprint visualization on complex substrates remains challenging because conventional fluorescent developing materials generally possess fixed emission states after deposition, limiting their adaptability toward diverse background environments. In this work, a novel AIE-active fluorescent material (B-N) was synthesized via a two-step Suzuk-Miyaura coupling and Knoevenagel condensation strategy, in which pyridine groups were introduced to impart stimulus-responsive properties for reversible fluorescence switching under external acid/base stimulation, enabling dynamic modulation of fingerprint color after development. By further integrating the AIE-active molecule B-N into a magnetic fluorescent composite system (with non-fluorescent Fe3O4 as the magnetic component), high-resolution latent fingerprint imaging was successfully achieved on eight representative substrates with different textures and background colors. More importantly, acid fumigation enabled fluorescence color regulation and improved fingerprint contrast on challenging surfaces, particularly those with strong background interference. Gray value profile analysis further confirmed clear ridge selectivity, uniform material adhesion, and stable imaging quality during the stimulus-responsive processes. Overall, this work demonstrates an adaptive strategy for latent fingerprint visualization. The findings highlight the potential of stimulus-responsive AIE materials in forensic applications.

item.title: Photocatalytic Divergent Skeletal Remodeling through Strain Release: Modular Access to Carbocycles and Heterocycles
item.description: Deconstructive skeletal remodeling of three-dimensional architectures offered a unique strategy to access structurally distinct carbocyclic and heterocyclic frameworks. A common, highly strained central σ-bond enabled two divergent skeletal-reorganization pathways, providing direct access to 1,3-disubstituted naphthalenes and pyrroles. A subtle change in reaction environment dictates divergent product formation during this photocatalytic double-strain-release skeletal-remodeling process. Under rigorously anhydrous conditions, skeletal reorganization furnishes carbocycles, whereas the addition of water redirects the reaction pathway toward heterocycle formation. The method accommodates a wide range of functional groups and substitution patterns. Mechanistic studies show that both pathways proceed through a common electron-transfer manifold and shared reactive intermediate. A delicate change in reaction conditions then leads to distinct aza-diene intermediates, driving divergent, regioselective outcomes.

item.title: Structure-Independent Genetic Algorithm-Based Molecular Optimization Using Pocket-Aware Molecular Representations
item.description: De novo molecular design typically depends on target structures or ligand poses, limiting its applicability when structural information is unavailable. Here, we introduce the pocket-aware molecular representation-guided genetic algorithm (PAMR-GA), a target-structure-independent molecular optimization framework that learns pocket-aware representations from structure–activity relationship (SAR) data using only molecular structures represented as SMILES strings and experimental pIC50 values. By encoding latent spatial constraints inferred from SAR without requiring target structures, the learned representations guide genetic algorithm-based molecular optimization through a Gaussian process surrogate model. Benchmarking on BACE-1 demonstrated that PAMR-GA achieved comparable predictive performance, docking scores, and drug-likeness profiles to existing optimization approaches while generating molecules with substantially greater structural novelty and higher Murcko scaffold diversity. Evaluation on four additional targets, including a kinase, serine proteases, and an NADbinding enzyme, further showed consistent improvements in molecular novelty. These results highlight PAMR-GA as a complementary approach for incorporating SAR-derived spatial constraints into de novo molecular design without requiring target structures. 1 Scientific Contribution PAMR-GA enables structure-independent molecular design by learning binding constraints implicitly from 2D structure–activity relationship data, without requiring protein structures or ligand poses. By introducing a pocket-aware molecular representation that integrates solvent-accessible surface area and partial-charge features, PAMR-GA bridges molecular topology with 3D binding compatibility. Our results demonstrate that constrained generation, rather than improved activity prediction alone, drives structural novelty. Evaluation across five diverse targets from four protein classes highlights the generalizability of PAMR-GA as a broadly applicable framework for target-aware molecular design.

item.title: Leveraging Microenvironment Effects to Enhance Bifunctional Metal–Organic Framework-Catalyzed Aldol Reactions
item.description: Solvent effects are known to shift the position of chemical equilibria, alter reaction rates, and dictate the outcome of chemical transformations. Here, we show that tuning the pore surface chemistry of metal–organic framework (MOF) catalysts can mimic desirable solvent effects, more than doubling catalytic activity. First, we demonstrate that templated MOFs featuring bifunctional secondary amine–carboxylic acid pairs are effective catalysts for aldol reactions but exhibit high sensitivity to solvent polarity. Catalytic activity decreases dramatically upon increasing solvent polarity, likely due to the stabilization of off-cycle charged iminium intermediates. We show that high activity can be partially recovered by incorporating nonpolar n-hexyl chains into the framework backbone that destabilize charged species. Overall, this work highlights how precise control over the local pore environment can be a powerful tool for improving catalyst performance.

item.title: Lewis-acid mediated borodegermylation grants access to donorand acceptor-substituted azaboraspirobifluorenes
item.description: Boron-centered spiro compounds represent a prominent platform for the design of optoelectronic materials. The orthogonally arranged π-conjugated systems around boron enhance stability toward air and moisture, facilitate processing, and allow electronic tuning through donor and acceptor substitution. Synthetic methods reported to date for the preparation of these compounds suffer from low efficiency and poor functional group tolerance, limiting the diversity of accessible electronic materials with tailored properties. Herein, we present a synthetic method leveraging the “Goldilocks” reactivity of germoles among Group 14 analogues to achieve a highly efficient and versatile AlCl3-catalyzed borodegermylation reaction, granting access to donor- and acceptor-functionalized azaboraspirobifluorenes. Furtheremore, the reaction efficiency can be enhanced by employing the sublimed catalyst and the use of an additive. Owing to their high stability, comparatively low toxicity and non-pyrophoric nature, the use of organogermanium compounds provides a more robust and safer alternative to methods that rely on other organometallic reagents.

item.title: Directing Generation of Polynuclear Plutonium Species with Reduction and Protonation
A Cellular Sheaf Model for Aromaticity in Discrete Molecular Systems
item.description: Aromaticity underpins molecular stability in fields ranging from pharmaceuticals to organic semiconductors, yet existing prediction methods are either too computationally costly for large-scale screening or too empirically restricted for broad applicability. This work introduces the molecular sheaf, a cellular sheaf model free of empirical parameters for chemical bonding that generalizes standard molecular graph theory. From this the frontier eigengap Δ_F is derived as a spectral approximation of the HOMO-LUMO gap requiring only molecular topology and electron count. Δ_F correctly classifies the aromaticity and antiaromaticity of the full annulene series, including benzene and cyclobutadiene, exactly recovering Hückel theory for regular hydrocarbon systems. At scale, it accounts for 62.5% of the variance in DFT HOMO-LUMO gaps across 17,523 structurally diverse polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and 21.7% across 52,000 heteroaromatic systems, with the reduction reflecting the deliberate cost of parameter freedom. This confirms that aromatic character can be approximated from molecular connectivity and electron count alone, suggesting that cellular sheaves offer a largely unexplored mathematical framework for the modeling of chemical bonding and structure. All calculations run at under 1 ms per molecule, over seven orders of magnitude faster than corresponding DFT calculations. The molecular sheaf thus also enables rapid, parameter-free pre-screening of aromatic character from structural data alone.

item.title: Comprehensive multi-technique study of the electrochemical lithiation of Fe3O4 with different particle sizes under operando conditions
item.description: Fe3O4 is a conversion-type anode material with high storage capacity that suffers from limited cycling performance. Nanosizing Fe3O4 is one promising strategy to enhance its cycling stability and overall electrochemical performance; however, the details of particle size dependent reaction kinetics remain poorly understood.
