We investigate the conversion reactions of bulk- and 50 nm-sized cubic Fe3O4 particles as active material using a multi-technique approach, by combining operando XRD, SAXS and magnetometry techniques. The results from the operando XRD and SAXS indicate that during initial lithiation reaction, the bulk electrode undergoes phase reduction with amorphization and formation of metallic iron nanograins, whereas the nanoparticle Fe3O4 retains its ccp oxygen anion framework throughout the lithiation process, hindering structural breakdown and amorphization and delaying the the growth of metallic iron nano grains. Operando vibrating sample magnetometry isused to cross-check the transformation and presence of metallic iron nanodomains owing to its unique sensitivity to local structural details hidden in conventional XRD. The reaction products were found to differ when time-resolved investigations are compared to ex-situ prepared specimens. These results highlight the critical importance of integrating complementary operando techniques to ex situ methods, to capture particle size–dependent lithiation pathways and relaxation mechanisms in conversion-type electrodes.

item.title: Acetylene as a C2 bridge for modular 1,4-dicarbonyl synthesis
item.description: Acetylene is among the cheapest and most abundant C2 feedstocks, yet catalytic methods that exploit both of its π-bonds remain scarce, and its use in fine-chemical synthesis is 15 confined largely to mono-functionalization. Here we report the traceless bridging of aldehydes and formamides with a single acetylene molecule through a catalytic double hydroacylation, in which direct hydrogen-atom transfer generates acyl and carbamoyl radicals without decarbonylation or any sacrificial group. Coupling of two identical radicals assembles 1,4-diketones and 1,4-diamides in a single operation, whereas the sequential 20 delivery of two different radicals provides unsymmetrical 1,4-dicarbonyl products with good cross-selectivity. The transformation accommodates aromatic and aliphatic aldehydes and diverse formamides, proceeds under mild conditions with 100% atom economy, and requires

item.title: A Decade of Progress: Quantifying Air Pollution Reductions in West Oakland, CA with Hyperlocal Monitoring
item.description: West Oakland is a disadvantaged community in California that has historically experienced a high and disproportionate exposure to diesel air pollution due to its proximity to major transportation infrastructure, including the Port of Oakland and several interstate freeways. However, years of community activism, statewide regulation and targeted local emissions mitigation have altered these conditions. In 2025/26, we replicated a 2015/16 mobile monitoring campaign that characterized hyperlocal spatial gradients in diesel air pollution by repeatedly sampling every road within the community. By comparing how concentrations changed in both magnitude and location, we study the impact of the different mitigation strategies across the last decade. Community wide, weekday daytime black carbon (BC) and NOx concentrations fell by 59.5% [54.2-64.6] (-0.51 μg m-3) and 60.0% [54.0-65.7] (-22.0 ppb) respectively, with near uniform fractional declines across seven community identified high impact residential zones (57-62% for BC, 52-64% NOx). This reduction is consistent with California’s aggressive statewide diesel truck regulations, a phased transition completed in 2023, under which every truck operating within the state must use diesel particulate filter and selective catalytic reduction exhaust treatment technologies. Concentration reductions on individual roads scaled linearly with measured truck traffic (R2 ~ 0.9), while roads in and around the Port show BC reductions beyond those expected from truck traffic alone, consistent with local investment in cleaner off road equipment. Overall, the decade’s changes avoided an estimated excess lifetime cancer risk from diesel particulate matter of 269 [209-328] per million for those who grow up in the community, and cut absolute disparity in exposure between the most and least polluted zones by 70% for BC and 58% for NOx. These results demonstrate the measurable air quality benefits associated with sustained emissions control and provide quantitative evidence of progress towards goals identified through decades of community-led monitoring and advocacy.

item.title: Editing-site selection for constrained QED improvement through frozen GenMol remasking
item.description: Shallow network, boosted decision-tree and graph-attention models were trained on a remaskingsite selection task utilizing the GenMol generator and a subset of bioactive molecules (30,000 training and 5,000 validation) from the ChEMBL 37 dataset. Models learned to optimize fragment selection policies by maximizing the fraction of successful remasked candidates, with success contingent on an increase in the RDKit quantitative estimate of drug-likeness (QED) under several chemical constraints. All three models show a marked increase in generation of at least one successful derivative out of 16 remasking runs on a held-out test set comprising 5,000 bioactive molecules: 66.0%–66.9%, 67.0%–67.4% and 66.3%–66.7% for the shallow network, boosted decision-tree and graph models, compared to 54.8%–55.6% for a fixed policy selecting the largest fragment (one-sided bootstrap 𝑝 < 10−4 for all models). A trivial baseline, selecting fragments randomly, displays 47.3% success. The fraction of valid candidates produced by all policies is about 99%. Analysis of learned policies showed consistent trends among the three models. Selection is biased toward larger pendants. Additionally, pendant selection shows several trends conditioned on the pendant-side, but not core-side, attachment atom. Larger carbon-and oxygen-attached fragments are selected more often (two-sided binomial 𝑝 < 10−10 in every model); a reversed tendency, albeit not statistically significant (𝑝 ≈ 0.02–0.30), is observed for nitrogen attachments. Controlling for fragment size, learned policies show preference for pendant-side nitrogen over oxygen and carbon, and for both chlorine and bromine over fluorine and carbon. Only LightGBM displays a statistically significant (two-sided exact binomial 𝑝 < 0.01) preference for sp2 over sp3 hybridization of pendant-side carbon atoms. At equal size, carbonyl-attached pendants are preferred to hydrocarbons.

item.title: Cu-Catalyzed Enantioconvergent Synthesis of N-Alkyl Amides from Racemic Alcohols
item.description: Enantioconvergent amidation of racemic alcohols offers a powerful retrosynthetic disconnection to convert abundant, readily accessible alcohol feedstocks into chiral N-alkyl amides, while streamlining access to valuable enantioenriched primary amines. However, a mechanistic framework that can integrate efficient C(sp3)–O bond cleavage with enantioselective amidation has remained understudied. Herein, we report the enantioconvergent deoxygenative amidation of racemic alcohols through a Cu-catalyzed radical relay. β-Scission of oxidant-derived electrophilic alkoxy radicals was leveraged as a radical-umpolung event, producing nucleophilic methyl radicals that effectively activate alcohol substrate-derived xanthates. Computation-guided optimization revealed that increasing xanthate electrophilicity facilitates methyl-radical addition and improves reaction efficiency. The transformation accommodates a variety of alcohols and amides with high enantioselectivity, and the reaction conditions are compatible with medicinally relevant functional groups, heterocycles, and pharmaceutical frameworks. Synthetic applications of this protocol streamline access to enantioenriched β-amino alcohols and biologically active primary amines, circumventing the need for enantioenriched alcohol precursors. Mechanistic studies revealed that polarity matching favors the capture of electron-deficient carbon-centered radicals by electron-rich CuII–amidates. Under catalytic conditions, however, the greater acidity of electron-deficient amides facilitates transmetalation, accelerating the formation of CuII–amidate and enhancing coupling efficiency.

item.title: Text-mined dataset of sol-gel synthesis protocols with phase purity outcomes using large language models
item.description: Sol-gel synthesis is a versatile method for producing inorganic materials that offers advantages such as atomic-level mixing and lower processing temperatures over traditional solid-state methods. Despite these benefits, achieving phase purity remains a challenge due to the process's sensitivity to synthesis parameters such as precursor choice, solvent selection, and heating conditions. Negative results, such as phase-impure outcomes, are essential for understanding sol-gel reaction pathways, but are largely absent from existing curated datasets. This work leverages Gemini 3.0 Flash to construct a text-mined inorganic sol-gel database with phase purity information. The dataset contains ~148,000 synthesis records, including ~28,000 phase-impure entries. All extracted entities achieved F1 scores greater than 0.89. At the record level, 68% of extracted records match human annotation on all evaluated fields. Furthermore, to validate the scientific utility of our dataset, we demonstrate that the aggregated data reproduces previously reported phase-purity trends for BiFeO3 thin films.

item.title: Atomic Layer Deposition of Ferroelectric HfxZr(1-x)O2 from Metal-β-diketonate Precursors with Fine Cation Tunability.
item.description: HfxZr1-xO2 (HZO) is a promising ferroelectric material for next-generation neuromorphic devices, where precise compositional control and complementary metal-oxidesemiconductor (CMOS) compatible processing are critical. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is particularly attractive for HZO integration due to its excellent conformality for future three-dimensional device architectures and possibility to control the composition. However, many widely used Hf and Zr precursors suffer from limited volatility and thermal stability. In this work, we exploit the robustness and favourable growth rates of the β-diketonate precursors Hf(thd)4 and Zr(thd)4 (thd = 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-3,5heptanedionate) - with ozone co-reactant – to demonstrate the ALD growth of binary HfO2, ZrO2, and ferroelectric HZO thin films with finely controlled Hf/Zr cation ratios enabling the Hf/Zr composition required for ferroelectric thin films. Optimized binary ALD processes yield low growth-per-cycle (GPC) values of 0.085 Å/cycle for HfO2 and 0.12 Å/cycle for ZrO2, these low GPCs enable fine and reproducible control of the Hf:Zr

item.title: Cross-flow microfluidic photocatalysis with metal-organic framework thin films
item.description: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) offer tunable reaction space, and using them as porous photocatalysts also allows the catalyst to be recovered and reused. In practice, though, performance is often constrained by how quickly reactants diffuse through the porous material and how well light reaches the active sites. In this work, we present an approach that pairs a MOF thin-film photocatalyst with a cross-flow microfluidic reactor. The thin film sets a well-defined diffusion length, the transparent thin film let light reach the active layer, and crossflow microfluidics allow diffusion control. Together, these features give control over reactant transport and improve illumination of the photocatalyst. To build the photocatalyst, we noncovalently load Ru(bpy)3(PF6)2 (bpy = 2,2′-bipyridine) into mesopores created by defects in a hierarchically porous Zr-based UiO-66 thin film. The well-established aerobic oxidation of ethyl 2-bromo-2-phenylacetate to ethyl 2-oxo-2-phenylacetate serves as a benchmark reaction; it is a test case rather than the main finding of the study. Under cross-flow conditions, the photocatalyst reaches a turnover frequency about ten times that of the equivalent MOF powder system, and it also outperforms the homogeneous benchmark. These findings highlight cross-flow microfluidics as a promising strategy for managing both mass transport and light delivery in MOF-based photocatalysis.

item.title: Generic aspects of neutral polymer brush bilayers immersed in an implicit solvent under steady-state shear
item.description: Using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with a Langevin thermostat, I study polymer brush bilayers immersed in an implicit solvent under steady-state shear. I use high-precision MD simulations, with 5×104 sampling steps, to measure the stress tensor, viscosity, kinetic friction coefficient, and chain extension as functions of the shear rate. The results show that the shear stress scales linearly with the Weissenberg number, Wi, over the entire range studied. The normal stress decreases without following a universal power law. The lateral chain extension decreases up to a critical value of Wi and then increases. The normal chain extension scales as Wi−0.3. The viscosity remains constant, whereas the kinetic friction coefficient increases without following a universal power law.

item.title: Electrostatic preactivation, a missing step in dioxygen activation
item.description: Dioxygen is the oxidant of aerobic life, yet most closed-shell molecules are stable in its presence.1–4 Conventional accounts of dioxygen activation begin with electron transfer to O2, typically from a redox-active metal centre or cofactor.5–9 Here we show that preparing dioxygen to receive that electron is a separate function, discharged by the electrostatic environment alone, and that the two can be tuned independently. At the equilibrium geometry of neutral O2 the anion that must receive the electron is unbound;10,11 a Lewis-acidic field removes this obstacle before any charge moves, a stage we term preactivation. Point charges alone split the O2 π* manifold and bind the anion at the neutral geometry. Reaction-path calculations show that inner-sphere electron transfer from the Zn–C bond, which generates a superoxide/alkyl-radical pair without metal-centred redox chemistry, is rate-determining. Calibrated on dialkylzincs alone, the in-plane anisotropy of the field gradient, with one term in the charge and distance of the metal resolved within the same series, predicts the π* splitting to within 7% in four enzyme active sites containing iron, copper, nickel or no metal. The electrostatic contribution of an enzyme active site to preactivation can thus be quantified on a scale calibrated with redox-silent organozinc compounds.

item.title: A dipole-forbidden conduction-band transition and the mid-infrared absorption of n-type Mg2Si, Mg2Ge and Mg2Sn: all-electron quasiparticle self-consistent GW calculations
The Mechanical Bond Reveals Hidden Interrupted Click Reactions
item.description: The CuI-triazolide intermediate of the Cu-mediated alkyne-azide cycloaddition (CuAAC) typically undergoes rapid proto-demetallation but can be intercepted by suitable coupling partners to give 5-substituted triazole products. However, the scope of such “interrupted click” reactions is restricted because some partners react too slowly to outcompete proto-demetallation or even actively promote the decomposition of the CuI-triazolide in preference to the desired coupling. Here we show that mechanical stabilisation of a CuI-triazolide within a [2]rotaxane can allow otherwise unproductive “hidden” interrupted click reactions to proceed; the triazolide intermediate of the active template CuAAC reaction couples with cyanide and primary amines under oxidative conditions to install these groups at the triazole 5-position in up to 99% yield. In contrast, the interlocked triazolide reacts slowly with some typical interrupted electrophiles that intercept non-interlocked CuI-triazolides. Based on these reactivity trends, we propose that the mechanical bond prevents direct attack of electrophiles on the Cu-C bond, instead enforcing inner-sphere reactivity at the CuI centre with a CuI/CuIII/CuI redox cycle. The C-5 substituent leads to a new source of mechanical positional isomerism and a suitably designed macrocycle can be removed after the coupling, allowing the interlocked architecture to serve as an auxiliary for products of otherwise inaccessible interrupted click reactions.

item.title: Fully Automated System for Exploring Molecular Dynamics Trajectories
item.description: Molecular dynamics (MD) studies often require separate tools for system preparation, simulation, enhanced sampling, analysis, and reporting, creating opportunities for inconsistent settings and undocumented decisions. We present FastMDXplora, an open-source Python framework built on OpenMM that integrates setup, simulation, analysis, and report phases through a single declarative configuration. A shared schema supports command-line and browser-based graphical interfaces. An optional artificial intelligence (AI) agent generates study configurations from natural-language descriptions, subject to the same validation as user-defined configurations. Each phase records its resolved settings, software versions, and execution environment. When a requested result lacks sufficient support, the software withholds it and reports the reason through a registry of 111 typed refusal codes. Fifteen estimator tests recover analytical benchmarks, including statistical inefficiencies within 2 % of reference values and WHAM reconstruction of analytical free-energy profiles from synthetic umbrella-sampling data with root-mean-square errors below 0.1 kJ mol−1. A labeled corpus of 25 defective and 26 clean studies produces the expected outcomes in all 51 cases. Calibration against ten replicas shows that singlerun standard errors at 20 ns can be up to tenfold smaller than replica-based estimates, even when the estimated correlation time is resolved. The software withholds standard errors when its correlation diagnostics fail, but passing these diagnostics does not establish calibrated uncertainty. In a trypsin–benzamidine case study, interaction analysis reveals differences in the engagement of Asp189 between two ligand charge states that are not distinguished by total contact counts. FastMDXplora provides an integrated framework for reproducible MD studies, combining workflow automation with explicit validation and provenance while preserving the need for independent assessment of sampling and uncertainty. The source code is available at https://github.com/aai-research-lab/FastMDXplora.

item.title: De Novo Design of Enantioselective Artificial Metalloenzyme Photocatalysts Containing Metal Polypyridine Cofactors
item.description: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins. In this study, we show that generative protein design can be harnessed to create de novo scaffolds that selectively accommodate one enantiomer of a metal polypyridine photocatalyst as a cofactor. The resulting ArMs enable efficient, enantioselective photocatalysis, highlighting a broadly applicable route for programming stereocontrol into metalloenzyme catalysts. High total turnover numbers are achieved, the ArMs can be recycled by simply extracting reaction products and reusing the aqueous ArM solution for subsequent reactions, and even commercially available racemic cofactor can be used for ArM formation. Transient Absorption characterization revealed that improvements to catalysis result from the increased quantum yield and excited state lifetime of the cofactor upon binding and substrate binding proximal to the cofactor within the ArM active site, which controls reaction stereoselectivity and the mechanism of energy transfer involved in photocatalysis. The simplicity of this approach could help transition ArM research out of a small group of specialist labs to any capable of expressing synthetic genes and working with commercially available metal complexes.

item.title: Thermo-photo catalytic partial oxidation of methane on hematite nanosheets functionalized with silver nanoparticles
item.description: Converting reactions driven by thermocatalysis to thermo-photo catalysis can offer several advantages, such as allowing the reaction to proceed under less harsh conditions to improve stability and tune reaction selectivity. Here, we report on using a dilute loading of silver nanoparticles on high surface area hematite nanosheets, an earth-abundant material, to transform our demonstrated thermocatalytic conversion of methane to a thermo-photo conversion of methane with lowered onset temperatures and a shift in reaction mechanism. With a dilute loading of spherical silver nanoparticles, reaction onset temperatures were lowered to 150 °C from 300 °C. Additionally, reaction products were shifted to CO, decreasing the selectivity toward CO2 and suggesting novel mechanistic pathways. The catalysts demonstrate great stability, with only a corresponding 4.9% and 11.3% decrease in activity over the bare and decorated catalyst over 15 hours. The fundamental relationships between reaction conversion and temperature, light intensity, and light wavelength studied in this work are important for providing a guideline for tuning other reactions with thermo-photo catalysis to improve catalyst conversion, selectivity, and stability.

item.title: Substituent Effects on the Photochemistry of Aqueous Phenolate-Based Anions Revealed by Extreme Ultraviolet Time-Resolved Photoelectron Spectroscopy
item.description: Phenolate (PhO-) is a prototypical chromophore and a recurring motif in photoactive biomolecular systems. Here, we use extreme-ultraviolet time-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (XUV-TRPES) to probe how para-substitution redirects the photophysics of aqueous 4-nitrophenolate (4NP-) and 4-chlorophenolate (4CP-) anions. In 4NP-, following 400 nm excitation, internal charge reorganization accompanied by nitrogroup torsion forms a stabilized twisted intramolecular charge-transfer (TICT) configuration in 74 fs, efficiently funneling the population through a conical intersection to the ground state within 200 fs. Similar dynamics are seen upon excitation at 240 nm, although the initially excited state is even shorter-lived (40 fs). No hydrated electron production is seen at either wavelength. In 4CP-, following 240 nm excitation of the S2 state, internal conversion to S1 occurs within 120 fs. Chlorine substitution introduces a competing 1πσ* dissociative channel whose potential energy surface intersects S1, but the higher S1/1πσ* crossing barrier relative to 4BP- allows the S1 population to survive long enough (25 ps) for solvent-assisted electron ejection and internal conversion. The dynamics thus resemble those of PhO- rather than the sub-picosecond dissociative relaxation of 4BP-. Taken together with our previous PhO- and 4-bromophenolate (4BP-) measurements, these results reveal how para-substitution across this prototypical series drives the accessibility of competing excited-state dynamical processes, leading to very different photostability and photochemistry.

item.title: Two extrapolation axes for many-body systems: interaction without an interaction module, chemical mixtures as the main example
item.description: We separate the extrapolation problem in many-body systems into two axes: toward combinations with more components, and toward components unseen. The prevailing pipeline—encode then interact—performs poorly when extrapolating in composition count. We propose a route that expresses interaction without an interaction module: a per-component encoder shaped by the task compresses interaction behaviour into each component’s encoding, and the encodings are combined and read out by a simple MLP. Where component identities are bounded while their combinations are not, this route performs better along the composition axis—a difference that follows from the underlying function form rather than from the data. Chemical mixtures are the main example, synthetic tasks isolate the two axes, and the same structure recurs in other fields.

item.title: Certifying the Kinetics of Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials from Single-Point Energies
item.description: Machine-learned interatomic potentials are validated by force errors on equilibrium configurations, yet activated rates depend on transition regions that equilibrium sampling rarely visits. In a onedimensional metastable double well, the worst-case rate sensitivity to force error grows as eβB/2 with barrier height B; a path-space bound valid at any friction shows that force error certifies rare-event frequencies only to within a factor that grows at the same rate. The leverage density weights energy errors by their influence on reactive transport: it is the normalised dissipation density of the reactive current. For reversible overdamped dynamics, the Dirichlet and Thomson principles give two-sided capacity bounds, converted to metastable rate bounds by basin population corrections. A path representation evaluates their averages from reactive trajectories, committor values and single-point energies. Sampling uses reference paths to assess sampled transitions and model paths to expose additional or overpopulated pathways. In alanine dipeptide, closely matched force errors produce rate changes from 0.49 to 3.5, consistent with estimated intervals. In Li3OCl, mechanism-resolved upper endpoints track six models’ vacancy-hop rates with a systematic underestimation of about 7%. Labels selected from both ensembles improve kinetics even as force errors rise. We propose reporting the energy-error contrast M between the leverage density and the basins, and the spread σν under the leverage density, alongside force error; both are independent of the energy zero.

item.title: Regioisomeric Engineering for Triplet Harvesting through Triplet–Triplet Annihilation
item.description: Three regioisomeric donor–acceptor–donor luminophores, 1DBF, 2DBF, and 3DBF, based on phenanthrene-9,10-dicarbonitrile (PHCN) acceptor and dibenzofuran (DBF) units, are designed to investigate regioisomer-dependent triplet exciton harvesting. The three emitters exhibit strong blue fluorescence in solution, with photoluminescence quantum yields of 63–87%, and show delayed fluorescence (DF) in both solution and solid states. Low temperature time-gated measurements, large singlet–triplet energy gaps, and concentration-dependent studies collectively support DF from triplet–triplet annihilation (TTA) mechanism rather than thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF). Notably, the substitution pattern strongly influences the excited state dynamics and triplet harvesting efficiency. Among the three regioisomers, 2DBF exhibits the most efficient TTA-derived DF, owing to favorable donoracceptor electronic coupling and a balanced contribution of 3LE and 3CT states, whereas the weaker coupling in 1DBF favors predominantly 3LE character, resulting in stronger phosphorescence and less efficient triplet harvesting through TTA. These results demonstrate that regioisomeric engineering can effectively modulate donor–acceptor electronic coupling and triplet state character, providing a useful molecular strategy for tuning the balance between DF and phosphorescence in organic emitters.

item.title: Supramolecular Preorganisation Enables Reversible Solid-state Photopolymerisation
item.description: Supramolecular preorganisation enables reversible solid-state photopolymerisation in an oligo(phenylenevinylene)-siloxane material. Photopolymerisation proceeds quantitatively in the ordered state but reaches only ~7% conversion in the disordered melt. Polymerisation disrupts columnar order and alters optical and local-current responses, while thermal depolymerisation largely restores the initial molecular and supramolecular state.

item.title: Realising a Poschenrieder dual-sector electrostatic analyser for charge-detection mass spectrometry
item.description: Megadalton biomolecular assemblies, including viral vectors, synthetic nanoparticles and protein aggregates, are increasingly important chemical and therapeutic entities, yet their heterogeneity often exceeds the resolving power and space charge tolerance of conventional mass spectrometry. To overcome these limitations, here we report the first realisation of a Poschenrieder dual-sector electrostatic analyser as a charge-detection mass spectrometer. The instrument traps individual ions in a continuous closed trajectory between two spherical electrostatic sectors, enabling induced-current detection over extended transients without end-cap deceleration. Coupled to a high-mass ion-transfer interface, the analyser supports both ensemble m/z measurements and single-particle charge detection of large biomolecular ions. We validate the platform using protein standards and demonstrate megadalton mass analysis of adeno-associated virus capsids, distinguishing empty and genome-containing populations in agreement with orthogonal mass photometry and Orbitrap-based measurements. Although charge-detection noise remains the principal performance constraint in this first-generation prototype, the dual-sector architecture offers a simple, high-capacity route to charge-detection mass spectrometry with substantial scope for improved resolution through miniaturisation and reduced detector capacitance.

item.title: Molecular Engineering of Fano Resonances for Enhanced Single-Molecule Thermoelectrics
item.description: Enhancing the thermoelectric power factor of single-molecule junctions requires simultaneously achieving high electrical conductance and thermopower, which are often mutually constrained. The sharp and asymmetric transmission features produced by Fano resonances offer a promising strategy for mitigating this trade-off. However, quantitative molecular structure–line-shape relationships linking molecular modifications to the resonance valley position and peak-valley energy width remain underexplored. Here, we demonstrate a molecular engineering strategy based on electronically tunable 9-fluorenylidene derivatives to tailor Fano resonance line shapes in single-molecule junctions. Systematic density functional theory and non-equilibrium Green’s function (DFT-NEGF) calculations reveal that substituent-induced variations in local orbital energies, backbone-side-chain coupling and localized-delocalized state detuning control the resonance valley position and the peak-valley energy width. Specifically, the valley position correlates linearly with the energy level of the side-group-localized LUMO, whereas the width is governed by the combined effect of main-side-chain coupling and localized-delocalized state detuning. Together, these two orbital descriptors provide a practical basis for the predictive molecular engineering of Fano resonance line shapes. To experimentally validate this strategy, we synthesized and characterized the designed dicyanomethylene-substituted derivative C-(CN)2 alongside a control molecule A-O. Electrochemically controlled scanning tunneling microscope break-junction (EC-STM-BJ) measurements confirm the emergence of Fano resonance features near the Fermi level for C-(CN)2, in agreement with the DFT-NEGF prediction, whereas no comparable features is observed for A-O. Crucially, statistical single-molecule conductance and thermopower measurements reveal that C-(CN)2 simultaneously exhibits higher conductance (G) and Seebeck coefficient (S) than A-O, overcoming the usual trade-off between these two parameters. This synergy effect yields a 97.6% enhancement in thermoelectric power factor (GS2) relative to control systems. By establishing explicit structure–line-shape–property relationships, this work provides a practical molecular engineering strategy for engineering Fano resonances in single-molecule thermoelectrics.

item.title: Emergence of Temporally Irreversible Hierarchical Solid Patterns through Information-Bearing Field Evolution and History-Dependent Growth Arrest
item.description: Patterns are widespread in natural and synthetic systems. Their formation is often interpreted through diffusion-driven instabilities or static geometric constructions. While successful in many contexts, these frameworks struggle to encode the spatiotemporal growth history of independently nucleated domains and their resulting collective behavior, including temporal asymmetry and hierarchical pattern formation with progressive solidification. This study shows that the TRACE (Temporal Recording through Arrested Coupled Evolution) mathematical model can generate intricate hierarchical patterns of solidifying and growing domains from simple, local growth rules through a phase information event-driven discretization operator within continuously evolving spatial information-bearing fields. The framework reveals how competition between growing domains can transform simple initial conditions into diverse final patterns, offering a new perspective on the emergence of spatial complexity from local growth processes, as observed experimentally in hierarchical pattern formation with solidification from fixed nuclei. This model suggests that complex patterns can emerge from the interaction of local, time-evolving growth, kinetic arrest rules with irreversible solidification embedded in front propagation. Numerical simulations reveal emergent patterns from the only TRACE equation, such as cell-like domains, stripes, banded structures, and hierarchical boundaries arising from variations in spatial confinement, nucleation timing, and domain density. The TRACE model also qualitatively reproduces the reported hierarchical macroscopic pattern formation observed in a chemical system. With these results, a phenomenon for growth-based natural patterns with solidification, and the featured characteristics of resultant patterns via growth and exclusion of each local cell are proposed.

item.title: PolycIMS: Polymers for Automated Cyclic Ion Mobility Spectrometry Calibration
item.description: The development and commercialization of cyclic ion mobility spectrometry (cIMS) instruments has considerably expanded the level of structural details that can be accessed for gaseous ions. Commercial cIMS instruments rely on travelling wave ion mobility spectrometry (TWIMS), a technique that requires calibration of the measured arrival times to enable the determination of collisional cross sections (CCS). Most calibration strategies use peptide mixtures that span a CCS range of approximately 100 – 400 Å2, which can introduce significant inaccuracies when extrapolating to larger ion structures. In addition, TWIMS calibration remains a tedious data processing step that would greatly benefit from automation.Here, we introduce polycIMS, a command-line tool that automates cIMS calibration and generates charge-independent calibration curves covering a broad CCS range from 100 – 1500 Å², within just 3 minutes on a standard laptop. Calibrated CCS can be determined in He or N2 (TWCCSN2→He, TWCCSN2→N2) using inexpensive, commercially-available polymer standards and are validated against reported values for more than 50 reference ions. Furthermore, the derived calibration parameters are largely insensitive to collisional activation, making it possible to calibrate multistage cIMS workflows such as slice collision induced unfolding (CIUn). We anticipate that the simplicity and accessibility of polycIMS will encourage its adoption as a new standard for cIMS calibration.

item.title: Comparative Characterization of Nitrogen–Nitrogen Bond-Forming Piperazate Synthases to Improve Activity and Precision
item.description: Piperazate synthases (PZSs) have recently gained attention as enzymes that catalyze the formation of nitrogen-nitrogen bonds, offering a sustainable alternative to traditional synthesis of substituted hydrazines. Although progress has been made in elucidating their structure and mechanism, an exhaustive study characterizing multiple PZSs regarding their activity or tendency toward side reactions under varying conditions has yet to be conducted. In this study, we profiled the activity of eight purified PZSs under 80 different conditions each, covering pH, buffers, salinity, temperature dependence, and thermal stability, using automated liquid handling and a colorimetric substrate consumption assay. We also performed kinetic and structural analysis of the two most promising PZSs and used LC-MS to quantitatively investigate the substrate scope and side reactions. Among the investigated enzymes, we identified two highly active synthases, SbPZS from Streptomyces sp. B93 and SgPZS from Streptomyces griseochromogenes. Both enzymes tolerated a broad range of reaction conditions, but differed in their side-product formation rates. We found this tendency to be sequence-dependent and controlled by pH. These findings provide detailed information regarding the in vitro applicability of PZSs and will improve their use in (chemo-)enzymatic cascades for synthesizing pharmaceutical building blocks.

item.title: Spin-Selective Charge Flow Drives Ultrafast Magnetic Transitions in Type-II Bipolar Magnetic Heterostructures
item.description: Ultrafast laser-driven changes in magnetic order provide a rich early-time platform for nonequilibrium physics. Established mechanisms and verified material candidates for ultrafast magnetic transitions in semiconducting magnets remain limited. Using density-functional theory (DFT) and real-time time-dependent DFT simulations, we demonstrate that spin-selective charge transfer across van der Waals layers, enabled by type-II bipolar band alignment, offers a robust way to control the magnetic order on the femtosecond timescale. In a representative CrSBr/CrSCl heterostructure, an antiferromagnetic-to-ferrimagnetic transition can be triggered within 40-56 fs under laser excitation above 4.2 eV, generating a net magnetic moment of ~1 µB per unit cell. The transition originates from a spin-flip charge transfer from spin-up valence states in CrSBr into spin-down conduction states in CrSCl. The resulting asymmetric demagnetization stabilizes residual spin polarization in CrSCl and induces a net magnetic moment. Additionally, electronic anisotropy facilitates an optically polarization-dependent charge redistribution, showing the main contribution from surface Cl atoms upon b-polarized excitation, while under a-polarized excitation the donation stems from interfacial Cr atoms. Our findings of spin-selective interlayer charge flow based on band alignment and symmetry breaking present a general mechanism for ultrafast optical control of magnetic order in low-dimensional materials.

item.title: Site-selective Halogenation of Aromatic C-H Bonds via Electrocatalytic Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide Cofactor Regeneration
item.description: Flavin-dependent halogenases (FDHs) catalyze site-selective C–H halogenation of electron-rich aromatic compounds but rely on multienzyme cofactor-recycling systems to continuously supply reduced flavin (FADH2). Here, we establish an overpotential-driven, mediator-assisted bioelectrocatalytic strategy for FADH2 regeneration that eliminates auxiliary reductases, nicotinamide cofactors, and enzyme immobilization. Cyclic voltammetry confirmed the proton-dependent FAD/FADH2 redox couple (-0.42 V vs Ag/AgCl, 3.5 M KCl) and the competing oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). Bulk electrolysis involving the FDH RebH revealed that L-ascorbic acid suppresses ORR-derived species more effectively than conventional catalase/glutathione/superoxide-dismutase systems, increasing conversion of tryptophan to 7-bromotryptophan from 20% to 46% after 24 h at -0.7 V. Increasing the cathodic potential to -1.1 V improved yields to 64% without substantially improving the faradaic efficiency (FE~ 5%). Introducing redox mediators such as 2-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone (HNQ) and methyl viologen (MV2+) enabled the HNQ/FAD pair to achieve quantitative halogenation within 10 h (FE ~ 14%) and the MV2+/FAD pair within 12 h (FE ~ 9%), enabling production of 8.8 mg of 7-bromotryptophan in a scale-up reactor. Moreover, the HNQ/FAD system exhibited a kinetic isotope effect (KIE) of (kH/kD = 1.8) for product formation in H2O versus D2O, supporting proton involvement in productive FAD regeneration and potentially reflecting cooperation between mediator-assisted electron transfer and surface-adsorbed hydrogen (Hads) produced during the hydrogen evolution reaction in accelerating FADH2 formation. Extending this method to engineered RebH variant 4-V enabled halogenation of larger substrates, establishing a scalable electrochemical platform for FDH catalysis. These results establish how electron delivery, proton availability, and competing oxygen reduction govern productive electrochemical flavin regeneration and provide a scalable platform for FDH catalysis.

item.title: Lipid Matrix-Dependent Effects of Ceramide Enrichment on Cholesterol-Containing PSM and DLPC Membranes
item.description: Ceramide is a bioactive sphingolipid that can reorganize cholesterol-containing membranes, but how membrane properties change with increasing ceramide content in different lipid matrices remains unclear. Using Martini 3 coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, we examine cholesterol-containing PSM and DLPC membranes across a controlled palmitoyl ceramide (PCER) composition series at a single liquid-phase temperature. Increasing PCER fraction generally decreases area per lipid and increases lipid ordering, consistent with membrane condensation. However, the responses differ between matrices. In PSM/CHOL, PCER is accommodated within an already ordered environment, producing only modest membrane stiffening. In DLPC/CHOL, PCER leads to greater changes in local packing heterogeneity and lateral organization, accompanied by a nonmonotonic mechanical response. PCER enrichment also changes the positional and orientational distributions of cholesterol in a matrix-dependent manner. These results show that ceramide-induced condensation does not necessarily produce monotonic membrane stiffening and highlight the importance of the host lipid matrix in determining membrane structure and mechanics.

item.title: Reductive insertion of a trivalent metal leading to the isolation of Prussian blue-type EuIIIFe3[Fe(CN)6]3
item.description: Reductive insertion reactions selectively modify three-dimensionally bonded solid-state structures through the addition of an elemental metal by electronation of the host structure and insertion of the metal cation into the host cavities for charge balance. However, with rare exceptions, this class of reactions has been largely restricted to insertions of monovalent metals. The reductive insertion of divalent and trivalent metal ions is intrinsically limited by their very slow diffusion through a host lattice at low temperatures and instability of a host lattice in the presence of these metals at high temperatures. These limitations originate from strong coordination of multivalent guest species to anions within the host lattice. By using coordinatively saturated anions such as cyanide in Prussian blue analogues, only relatively weak coordination modes to guest cations are available within the host structures, suggesting these host structures may participate in multivalent metalations. Herein, we report reductive insertion of europium into Berlin green Fe[Fe(CN)6] under relatively mild conditions by reaction with EuI2 at 150 °C in N-methyl-2-pyrolidone. The formation of the half-ferrous product, EuIIIFe3[Fe(CN)6]3, is an exceptionally rare reductive insertion of a trivalent metal, and the first example of a phase pure Prussian blue (An+1/nFe[Fe(CN)6]; A = metal cation) isolated with either a lanthanide or multivalent A-site metal. The resulting compound exhibits a distribution of iron oxidation and spin states not observed in previously reported Prussian blue phases of the form MIFe[Fe(CN)6]. The valence of Eu3+ was confirmed by a combination of X-ray absorption, 57Fe Mössbauer, and magnetic susceptibility measurements, which informed a possible reaction mechanism invoking redox exchange between the ferrous host, Eu3+ guest ions, and excess Eu2+ in solution.

item.title: Ion Gradients Drive Flooding in Membrane-Electrode Assembly CO2 Electrolyzers
item.description: Low-temperature carbon dioxide electrolysis (CO2E) provides a low-carbon-emission pathway to basic chemical products. While anion exchange membrane (AEM)-based CO2E can provide high selectivity towards carbon products, runtimes are far below industry requirements. Flooding is a major obstacle to long-term stability as it limits CO2 access to the catalyst layer, but the reasons for continuous water fluxes to the cathode are poorly understood. Here we present a model-aided experimental analysis of the driving forces for flooding. By tracking high-frequency resistance, anolyte conductivity, and cathode water accumulation over 24-hour runtimes across a range of current densities, temperatures and anolyte concentrations, we reveal AEM ion gradients as the main driving force for both flooding and cation-crowding at the cathode catalyst. We then show how ion gradient management can maintain steady CO selectivity and increase maximum CO2E partial current densities, with temperatures acting as a primary factor in reducing ion gradients. Using these insights, we demonstrate stable CO production at 500 mA cm-2 on an ionomer-free Ag catalyst.

item.title: Tracing the Physical Roots of Chemical Concepts through Artificial Intelligence
item.description: The language of chemistry is universally based on simple concepts such as the atom and the bond. Yet, these concepts find no place in a physical description of the nanoscopic world, where–within a Born-Oppenheimer view–a molecule is ultimately represented by a three-dimensional mathematical function expressing the electron density surrounding a given set of nuclei. While several methods have been proposed over the past decades to define atoms and bonds through the analysis of the molecular electron density, consensus on a theory bridging chemical concepts to the underlying physics has not been reached, and this has corroborated the idea that chemical concepts have an intrinsic degree of vagueness. In this work, we harness the power of Artificial Intelligence to trace the physical roots of chemical concepts–from the simple idea of an atom or a bond, to more elaborate ones such as the particular ‘chemistry’ of an atom in a given molecular context–and assess to what extent these can be framed on a quantitative level. Using simple machinelearning models, we show that a computer can be successfully trained to discern the nuanced chemical character of atoms and bonds from compact representations of the electron density with an accuracy of 98 % and 99 %, respectively. These results indicate that elusive and articulated chemical concepts are actually hard-coded in the underlying physics and suggest that chemistry is less ‘fuzzy’ a science than is generally assumed.

item.title: Atomic layer deposition of germanium using a germanium(II) triazenide precursor and plasma electrons
item.description: Germanium (Ge) thin films were deposited by electron chemical vapor deposition (e-CVD) using bis(1,3-di-tert-butyltriazenide)germanium(II), Ge(triaz)2, and plasma electrons. Separating the Ge(triaz)2 pulse and electron exposure into sequential steps affords a controllable cyclic deposition process in which both precursor adsorption and electron exposure exhibited the self-limiting behavior characteristic of atomic layer deposition (ALD) process. 50 deposition cycles resulted in a continuous film with a thickness of 16 nm. The films were oxidized after exposure to air and low concentrations of carbon and nitrogen impurities were detected after Ar+ etching. The plasma decomposition of Ge(triaz)2 is found to render dinitrogen and volatile hydrocarbon fragments, explaining the low impurity levels of the deposited films.

item.title: When Ethylene Meets Sulfur: Direct Synthesis of Minimal Ethylene-Sulfur Copolymers
item.description: In inverse vulcanization chemistry, research has predominantly focused on multifunctional unsaturated comonomers to stabilize sulfur-rich structures, whereas the direct copolymerization of elemental sulfur with simple olefins has remained comparatively unexplored. Extending this concept to the simplest olefin, we report Minimal Ethylene-Sulfur Copolymers (MinESC), synthesized through the direct reaction of gaseous ethylene with elemental sulfur via a base-mediated inverse vulcanization approach under mild conditions. These materials are viscoelastic fluids of tunable viscosity reaching exceptionally high values. They exhibit a peculiar sheet-like morphology, polar surfaces, elevated electrical conductivity, and high permittivity, and can be reprocessed into predominantly elastic structures following thermal treatment. Our approach provides a straightforward route to a distinct class of sulfurethylene-derived functional materials and demonstrates that inverse vulcanization chemistry can be extended to the simplest olefin under industrially relevant pressures and temperatures.

item.title: Core-to-rim chemical zoning of a Paraíbatype tourmaline from Abulo, Ethiopia: Implications for origin determination
item.description: Copper-bearing tourmaline of Paraíba type is now mined at Abulo in southern Ethiopia. We report the core-to-rim characterisation of one colour-zoned crystal attributed to this locality, obtained in Bangkok in June 2026. A sawn slab about 12 mm across and 5 mm thick was e x t e n s i v e l y analysed by electron microprobe (113 points), LA-ICP-MS analysis (45 spots on two traverses and 58 isotopes, totaling 2,565 concentration values with silicon as internal standard and GSE and NIST 610 as external standards), LA-ICP-TOFMS imaging (13,500 measuring spots of 24 µm and 55 isotopes, totalling 729,000 concentration values with silicon as internal standard and GSE and NIST 610 as external standard, about 505,000 of them above limits of detection), Raman spectroscopy (24 spectra) and a screening test by ED-XRF. The crystal is an Al–Li tourmaline of the elbaite series, including elbaite, fluor-elbaite, and elbaite with a liddicoatite component. Of the rare earth elements, only the light rare earths, La to Sm, are present in the tourmaline's composition. Compared with our 2009 reference profiles for Brazil, Mozambique and Nigeria, the crystal from Ethopia has higher vanadium and gallium concentrations and evolves toward bismuth rather than manganese. Because the comparison is based on a very detailed analysis of five growth zones, the reported observations are very significant and represent more information than the analyses of larger sample sets. Therefore, this information is crucial as origin criteria.
